t.jebel wastani kafr aqareb@36.0,36.4:
Along the limestone uplands of north-western Syria, close to the Turkish border, lie the remains of hundreds of abandoned villages from late antiquity, the so-called Dead Cities. Kafr Aqareb, on the Jebel Wastani, is one of them, part of the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria listed by UNESCO in 2011. These were prosperous farming communities between roughly the first and seventh centuries, growing olives, grapes and grain, and producing oil that was traded across the Roman and Byzantine world. They built in stone, with remarkable skill: houses, churches, bath houses, olive presses and tombs, many still standing to roof height. When trade routes shifted and the region changed hands, the villages were gradually abandoned, leaving ghost towns that look as if their inhabitants left only recently.

The most famous of these sites is Qal'at Sim'an, the great church built around the pillar on which Saint Simeon Stylites lived for decades in the fifth century, preaching to crowds below. It was once one of the most important pilgrimage sites in the Christian world.

The honest truth is that this region is not a place to ride today. Syria has been devastated by years of civil war, and the north-west remains volatile and dangerous. Governments almost universally advise against all travel to the country, and the border with Turkey is closed to casual crossing. The Ancient Villages are on UNESCO's list of World Heritage in Danger, and some sites have suffered damage.

What you can do is approach from the Turkish side. The province of Hatay, around Antakya, the ancient Antioch, shares much of the same landscape and history, with olive groves, limestone hills and Roman and Byzantine remains. Antakya was badly damaged by the earthquakes of 2023, and the city is still rebuilding. The roads in Hatay range from fast highways to winding mountain routes, with views over the Orontes valley and the Amik plain.

Fuel, food and services are available in Turkish towns such as Reyhanlı and Antakya. Try künefe, a hot cheese pastry soaked in syrup, a speciality of Hatay, and keep a close eye on current travel advice for anywhere near the border.
t.fort jesus@-4.1,39.7:
Fort Jesus stands at the edge of Mombasa island looking out over the entrance to the old harbour, its thick coral-stone walls glowing ochre in the late afternoon. The Portuguese built it at the end of the sixteenth century, to a design by the Italian military architect Giovanni Battista Cairati, to secure their hold on the Swahili coast and the Indian Ocean trade. It changed hands repeatedly over the next two centuries, most famously after a siege by Omani Arab forces that lasted almost three years at the end of the 1690s, and later served as a prison. Since 2011 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the museum inside tells the story of the coast and its many rulers.

The Old Town next door is the soul of the place. Narrow streets wind between houses with carved wooden doors and balconies, mosques, spice shops and small cafés where men sip spiced coffee from tiny cups. The architecture mixes Swahili, Arab, Indian and Portuguese influences, a testament to Mombasa's long history as a port city connecting Africa to Arabia and India.

As a riding destination, Mombasa is not for the faint-hearted. The city is hot and humid, the traffic chaotic, with matatus, tuk-tuks, boda-boda motorbikes and trucks heading to and from the port. The island is linked to the mainland by bridges and the Likoni ferry, which can involve long queues. Once you leave the city, the coastal roads north toward Kilifi and Malindi or south toward Diani open up a bit, with palm trees, baobabs and glimpses of the ocean. Ride early in the morning, before the heat and traffic peak, and keep your wits about you.

Mombasa is Kenya's second-largest city, with all services, including fuel stations everywhere. The food is wonderful: biryani and pilau rich with spices, grilled fish with coconut sauce, mahamri doughnuts with chai for breakfast, and fresh mango or pineapple from the street vendors. Drink plenty of water, wear light clothing and sunscreen, and keep an eye on your bike and belongings in busy areas.
t.kaya kauma@-3.6,39.7:
The kayas are patches of forest scattered along the coast of Kenya, each one once the fortified village of a Mijikenda community, hidden deep in the trees for protection. The Mijikenda, nine related peoples of the coastal hinterland, later moved out of the forests, but the kayas remained sacred places, where elders held ceremonies, buried their leaders and made decisions, and where cutting trees or harming the forest was forbidden. That protection has preserved precious remnants of coastal forest, rich in rare plants and animals. In 2008, a group of them, including Kaya Kauma near Kilifi, was listed by UNESCO as the Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests.

Visiting a kaya means respecting its rules. Entry is controlled by the council of elders, and you should only go in with permission and a guide, often through a local community or conservation group. Some areas are off limits to outsiders altogether. Inside, the forest is dense and cool, with tall trees, lianas, birds and butterflies, and paths lead to clearings where ceremonies are held. Photography may be restricted, so always ask first.

Kilifi, about thirteen kilometres away, is a relaxed coastal town on a wide creek, crossed by a long bridge. It has a beautiful beach at Bofa, sailing on the creek, and the ruins of Mnarani, a medieval Swahili town with mosques and tombs, on a hill overlooking the water. Further north, the ruins of Gede, another Swahili town, hidden in the forest, are fascinating, and Malindi and Watamu have beaches, coral reefs and marine parks.

The riding along the coast is a mix of good tarmac on the main road between Mombasa and Malindi and rougher roads inland, with potholes, dust in the dry season and mud in the rains. Traffic includes matatus, trucks, tuk-tuks and boda-boda motorbikes, and pedestrians and animals are always on the roads. Ride carefully, especially at night, when unlit vehicles and obstacles are common. Kilifi has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try Swahili dishes such as pilau, coconut fish curry, or chapati with beans, and fresh coconut water from a roadside stall.
t.jebel barisha deiroune@36.2,36.7:
On the limestone ridge of Jebel Barisha, in north-west Syria near the Turkish border at Reyhanlı, lie the stone ruins of Deirouné, one of the hundreds of late Roman and Byzantine villages that UNESCO lists as the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, often called the Dead Cities. Between roughly the first and seventh centuries, farmers here grew olives and vines on the uplands, prospered, and built houses, churches and olive presses in finely cut stone. When the trade networks that sustained them collapsed, the villages were slowly abandoned, and the dry climate left them remarkably intact.

The landscape is stark and beautiful: grey limestone outcrops, red earth in the hollows, olive groves, and roofless basilicas standing against the sky. The ridges of Jebel Barisha, Jebel Sem'an and Jebel Zawiyé hold the densest concentration of these villages, and on a clear day you can see from one ridge to the next, a whole lost countryside spread out below.

The hard truth is that this is Idlib province, and the area has been at the centre of the Syrian war and its aftermath. Security, access and the state of the roads change quickly and depend on who controls what at any given moment. Many governments advise against all travel to Syria, insurance is usually void, and border crossings for private vehicles may be closed or restricted. If you are reading this as a plan, read the latest official travel advice first and take it seriously; this is not a place to improvise.

For most riders, Deirouné is for now a place to know about rather than to visit, and perhaps to see from the Turkish side, where Reyhanlı and the Hatay province offer fuel, food and the wider history of Antioch. Hatay's cuisine, with its spicy dips, künefe and pomegranate molasses, is reason enough to ride that far. If peace and access return, these ridges will be among the most extraordinary rides in the Middle East: slow, stony lanes through olive groves to Byzantine churches that look as if their congregations stepped out only yesterday.
t.the duruma kayas@-4.0,39.5:
Inland from Mombasa, where the coastal plain begins to climb towards the dry bush of the interior, small islands of dense forest stand out from the farmland and scrub. These are kayas, the sacred forests of the Mijikenda peoples, and the Duruma kayas belong to one of the nine Mijikenda groups. Together with others along the coast they were inscribed in 2008 as the Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests.

The kayas began as fortified villages in clearings deep in the forest, with paths winding through the trees to protect them from raiders. Over time people moved out to farm, but the kayas remained as ritual and burial places, governed by councils of elders who decide who may enter and under what conditions. Cutting trees, taking plants or even entering certain areas is forbidden, which is why these patches of coastal forest survived while the land around them was cleared. They shelter rare plants, birds and butterflies, and they are living religious sites, not parks.

That means a visit has to be arranged with respect. Approach through local elders or a recognised guide, ask before taking photographs and follow the rules you are given, which may include removing shoes or covering certain clothing. Without permission, enjoy the forests from the edges and the roads.

The main artery for anyone on wheels is the Mombasa to Nairobi highway, which passes through Mariakani, sixteen kilometres away. It is heavily used by trucks carrying containers from Mombasa port, and overtaking manoeuvres can be frightening. The smaller roads that branch off towards the kayas are often red murram, dusty in the dry season and slippery after rain. The coast has two rainy seasons, the long rains around April to June and the short rains around November, and the heat and humidity are constant.

Mariakani has fuel and food; Mombasa, with its Old Town, carved doors and the Portuguese Fort Jesus built at the end of the sixteenth century, has everything else. South of the city, the Shimba Hills offer cooler air, forest and elephants, and a good ride for an afternoon. Along the roadside, look for coconut stalls and palm wine sellers; a fresh madafu, coconut water drunk straight from the nut, is the best cure for the coastal heat.
t.jebel zawiye 1 ba uda@35.7,36.6:
On the limestone uplands of the Jebel Zawiya in north-western Syria, among olive groves and stony fields, stand the remains of villages abandoned more than a thousand years ago. They are part of the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, often called the Dead Cities, inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2011. Ba'uda is one of these sites, with houses, churches, tombs and presses built of finely cut stone between the first and seventh centuries, when the region grew rich on olive oil.

These villages are remarkable because they survived almost intact after they were abandoned, probably due to changing trade patterns and political upheaval. You can walk through streets, enter houses with their doors and windows still in place, and see churches with apses and columns. Pyramid-roofed tombs, like those at nearby al-Bara, are particularly striking. The quality of the stonework is extraordinary, and the light on the pale limestone in the evening is beautiful.

However, the situation in this area must be taken very seriously. The Jebel Zawiya was a front line in the Syrian civil war for years, and many villages, including ancient sites, suffered damage. Even after the change of government in late 2024, the region remains affected by destruction, unexploded ordnance, mines and an unpredictable security situation. Before considering any travel here, check current advice from your government and reliable local sources, and do not leave established roads and paths.

Kafranbel, six kilometres away, is a town that became known during the war for its creative protest banners. Services in the region are unreliable, and fuel may be scarce or of poor quality. If and when travel becomes safe, the riding would be through rolling limestone country with olive groves, small villages and views towards the Orontes valley and the mountains near the coast, where the great castle of Qal'at Salah ed-Din stands.

For now, the Dead Cities are perhaps best appreciated through books and photographs, and through the hope that they will one day welcome visitors again. Their survival over centuries is a testament to the skill of their builders, and their fate in recent years is a reminder of how fragile heritage can be.
t.ancient villages of northern syria@36.3,:
On the limestone hills west of Aleppo, hundreds of abandoned villages stand in a landscape of olive groves and stony fields, their houses, churches, oil presses and tombs built of finely cut stone between the first and seventh centuries. These are the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, often called the Dead Cities, listed by UNESCO in 2011. They were prosperous farming communities in the late Roman and Byzantine periods, growing olives and grapes for trade, and were abandoned for reasons still debated, perhaps changing trade routes and the political upheavals of the seventh century.

What remains is extraordinary: whole villages with houses still standing to their roofs in some places, churches with arched doorways and carved decoration, and baths and tombs scattered across the hills. The most famous site is the Church of Saint Simeon Stylites, built around the pillar where the saint lived for decades, and other remarkable buildings include the basilica of Qalb Lozeh, with its massive arches.

The past decade and more of war has had a heavy impact on the region. Parts of the area were fought over, some sites were damaged, and many were used as shelters by displaced people. Since the political changes of late 2024, the situation in Syria has been changing, but security risks, including unexploded ordnance and instability, remain serious concerns. Anyone considering a visit must check current official travel advice, travel with local knowledge and stay on established roads and paths.

In more peaceful times, the riding in this region was lovely: small roads winding through olive groves, over limestone hills and past villages, with ancient ruins appearing around every corner. The roads were narrow and sometimes rough, and the summers hot and dry, but spring, with wildflowers and green fields, was magical.

Nubl, about fourteen kilometres away, and the larger towns of the region have fuel and supplies, depending on the current situation. Syrian food is a pleasure anywhere: try fresh bread from a bakery, a plate of hummus, muhammara made with roasted peppers and walnuts, and a strong coffee. If and when the region is stable, the Dead Cities will once again be one of the most remarkable places in the Middle East to explore.
t.ancient city of aleppo@36.2,37.2:
Aleppo has a claim to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and for most of its history it was a great trading city at the western end of the Silk Road. Its old town, listed by UNESCO in 1986, grew around a massive citadel on a mound in the centre, ringed by a moat and entered through a fortified gateway and bridge, mostly the work of the Ayyubid rulers in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Around it lay the souqs, kilometres of covered markets, among the largest in the Middle East, and caravanserais, mosques, madrasas and fine courtyard houses.

The city suffered terribly during the war that began in 2011. Between 2012 and 2016, the old city was a front line, and much of it was badly damaged or destroyed, including large parts of the souqs and the eleventh-century minaret of the Umayyad Mosque, which collapsed in 2013. The earthquake of February 2023 caused further damage. Restoration work has since been under way on several monuments and parts of the souqs, but the scars are still evident everywhere.

Since the political changes of late 2024, the situation in Syria has been evolving. Security risks remain, and anyone considering travelling to Aleppo, let alone riding a motorcycle there, must check current official travel advice, travel with reliable local contacts and be prepared for unpredictable conditions. Infrastructure, including fuel supply and electricity, can be unreliable.

Aleppo is a big city, and riding in it is chaotic, with heavy traffic and damaged roads in places. The surrounding countryside is mostly flat, with farmland, olive groves and limestone hills to the west, where the Dead Cities lie, and the roads between them are narrow and sometimes in poor condition.

Aleppo is famous across the Arab world for its food. The city is known for its kebabs, especially kebab karaz, made with sour cherries, and for its muhammara, its pistachios and its sweets, and the Aleppo pepper, a mild, fruity chilli, is used in kitchens around the world. Aleppo soap, made from olive and laurel oils, is another famous product. When the time comes that the city is safe to visit again, sitting in a restored courtyard with a glass of tea and a plate of sweets will be one of the great pleasures of travel in the Middle East.
t.kaya ribe@-3.9,39.6:
Kaya Ribe is one of a string of sacred forests that sit on the low hills behind Kenya's coast, and the reason it exists says a lot about the people here. The Mijikenda, nine related communities, settled this coastal hinterland several centuries ago and built fortified villages, the kayas, in the forest. Today the village huts are mostly gone, but the forests remain, protected by councils of elders who treat them as the home of ancestors. A scatter of these kayas, Ribe among them, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

It matters how you approach it. These are living religious sites, not parks. You normally need a local guide or an introduction from the elders, you may be asked to dress modestly and leave things behind, and you should ask before taking photographs. In return, you get a cool, dim patch of mature forest with rare plants and birds, an astonishing contrast with the surrounding scrub and cassava fields. The nearby village of Rabai is also the site of the first Christian mission in East Africa, founded by the German missionary Johann Ludwig Krapf in the 1840s, and its old church is still standing.

The ride here from Mombasa is mostly on the main highway towards Nairobi, which is busy and dominated by heavy trucks hauling freight from the port. Mariakani, a market town some eighteen kilometres out, is the practical stop, with fuel, food and a lot of dust. Once you leave the tarmac, the tracks toward Rabai are red laterite, slippery in the rains of April and May and corrugated in the dry months. Heat and humidity here are intense, so start early and carry plenty of water.

The best seasons are January to March and again in July to October, when the sky is clear and the roads are firm. Mombasa itself has all the fuel and supplies you need, and its old town, with the Portuguese Fort Jesus, makes a good second half to the day. A ride out to the kayas is a quiet, modest outing, with more to see than first appears, and it rewards slow looking.
t.moscow@55.8,37.6:
Moscow does not do small. It has more than ten million people, a ring road, the MKAD, that encloses a space bigger than many countries' capitals, and a centre that is arranged in concentric circles like the rings of a tree. At the middle is the Kremlin, the red-brick fortress on the Moskva river, with its golden-domed cathedrals and its walls, and beside it Red Square, with the colourful domes of St Basil's. The city was first mentioned in the chronicles in 1147, and grew from a modest wooden stockade into the capital of a vast empire.

To ride in Moscow is to be reminded of its scale. The Garden Ring and the Third Ring carry huge flows of traffic, drivers are fast and aggressive, and motorcycles filter between lanes at speed. The best time to explore on two wheels is a summer evening, when the light lasts until late, the traffic eases, and the bridges over the river are lit. The skyscrapers known as the Seven Sisters, built under Stalin, rise from the skyline, and from Sparrow Hills, the high ground near the university, you can see the whole city spread out in a haze. The metro stations, designed as underground palaces, are worth leaving the bike for.

From the city, a favourite day trip leads north-east to Sergiev Posad, about seventy kilometres away, where the Trinity Lavra of St Sergius, the most important Russian Orthodox monastery, stands inside white walls with blue and gold domes. The road passes through forest and farmland, and pilgrims fill the monastery on holidays. It is a good outing for a long day, with plenty of cafes in the town and stalls selling painted wooden toys, a local craft.

Fuel is found everywhere in the city and along the main roads, and the cafes range from cheap canteens to fancy restaurants. Summers are warm and can be thunderous, while winters are long, dark and very cold, with snow from November to March. Before planning any trip, check the current travel and entry conditions carefully, as they change often and can affect insurance, border crossings and the practicality of riding in Russia.
t.kaya kambe@-3.9,39.7:
Inland from the Kenyan coast, behind the sugar-white beaches and the hotel strip, lie forests where the Mijikenda people have kept their sacred places for centuries. Kaya Kambe is one of them, a fragment of the old coastal forest around a clearing where the elders once had their fortified village, the kaya, and where they still hold ceremonies and settle disputes. The Mijikenda, whose name means nine homesteads, are nine related peoples, among them the Giriama, Digo, Rabai and Kambe, who by tradition migrated south from a place called Shungwaya a few hundred years ago and made these hilltop forests their strongholds. A group of the kayas was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2008.

The forests matter for nature as much as for culture, because the surrounding land has been cleared for farms, and the kayas, protected by custom, preserve some of the last patches of the ancient coastal forest of East Africa. They hold rare trees, birds and butterflies, and the ritual rule that nobody should cut wood or clear land without permission has been the best conservation tool on the coast.

Visiting is a matter of respect. The kayas are living sacred places, and you should arrange access through the local committee or an authorised guide, follow the rules on dress, shoes and photography, and never wander in alone. Women may be asked to cover their legs and everyone may be asked to leave certain items outside.

The ride from Mombasa runs along the main highway towards Nairobi, which is busy with heavy trucks, buses, and overtaking, and needs full attention at every moment. Go early, keep your lights on, and expect sudden speed bumps in the villages. Mariakani, a town of about thirteen thousand people, is the nearest place for fuel and food, and Mombasa, about twenty kilometres away, has everything else, including the old Portuguese Fort Jesus, built in the 1590s, and the narrow lanes of the Old Town. Cashew, mango and coconut trees line the side roads, and in the dry season the red dust coats everything. The coolest time is early in the day, and the long rains of April and May can turn the side tracks to mud.
t.yesiloz site@38.6,35.0:
Cappadocia was made by volcanoes and carved by people. Millions of years ago, the volcanoes of central Anatolia, Erciyes and Hasan, covered the plateau in thick layers of ash that hardened into a soft rock called tuff, and wind and water have since eroded it into the cones, pinnacles and ridges that are known as fairy chimneys. People found the rock easy to carve, and for thousands of years they have dug homes, churches, storerooms and whole underground cities into it. The area is a World Heritage site, and it is hard to find a corner without a cave or a dovecote cut into a cliff.

It lies in the quieter country south and east of Urgup, where the valleys are less crowded than Goreme, and where you can still find a rock church or a cave house that is not on any signboard. In the Byzantine period, from about the sixth to the eleventh centuries, monks and villagers decorated rock-cut chapels with frescoes, and the hidden valleys sheltered communities from Arab raids. The underground city of Kaymakli, on the ride, has eight levels, though only four are open, with ventilation shafts, stables, kitchens and rolling stone doors that could be closed against attackers.

The riding is pleasant and varied. The main roads are wide and smooth, and the side roads wind between vineyards, apricot orchards and fields of sunflowers and wheat, with the strange rock formations rising on every side. The best time of day is the early morning, when hot-air balloons rise over the valleys, a hundred or more at a time, and the light on the rock is soft. Winter brings snow and ice, and summers are hot and dry. Take care on gravel roads and watch for tractors and sheep.

Urgup has about sixteen thousand people and Goreme about six thousand, so fuel, food and rooms are no trouble. Taste the local pottery kebab, cooked in a sealed clay jug that is broken open at the table, and the local wines, since Cappadocia has produced wine since ancient times.
t.qal at salah el din@35.6,36.1:
Few castles are as dramatic as the one that sits on a spur of rock in the coastal mountains of Syria, between two deep ravines. Qal'at Salah El-Din, or Saladin's Castle, takes its name from the Muslim leader who captured it from the Crusaders in 1188 on his campaign along the coast, but the story is much older. The site was fortified in Byzantine times, taken by the Crusaders in the early twelfth century, and strengthened with new walls and towers. The great trench that separates the castle from the rest of the ridge is cut out of solid rock, many metres deep, and in the middle of it a slender needle of stone, about twenty-eight metres high, was left standing to carry the drawbridge. It is one of the great sights of medieval military architecture.

Inside are the remains of a keep, a Crusader chapel, a Muslim palace, a mosque and a water cistern, and the walls look over thick forest, with the sea shimmering in the distance. The surrounding hills are green and wooded, with oak, pine and fruit trees, a fragrant landscape quite unlike the desert that many imagine for Syria. The castle was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2006, along with the Crac des Chevaliers, as one of the finest surviving examples of Crusader and Islamic military architecture.

The country has been through more than a decade of war and its infrastructure and security are still unreliable in many places. Most governments advise against travel, insurance is unavailable, and conditions can change quickly, so anyone who is thinking about visiting should consult current official advice rather than any text like this. The castle's setting in the Jebel Ansariyah range, with winding forest roads between Latakia and the interior, was famed for its beauty, and Latakia, about twenty-five kilometres away, a port city of more than three hundred thousand, and Jableh, a smaller coastal city, were the main service towns.

For now, the castle is better known than visited, and it may be best admired in books and old photographs, until the day when travel becomes possible again.
t.jebel sem an 2 kafrnabo@36.4,36.9:
Northern Syria has a landscape of limestone hills crowded with the shells of ancient villages, and the Jebel Sem'an, the Mountain of Simeon, is the heart of it. Between the fourth and seventh centuries, when this region was a prosperous corner of the late Roman and then Byzantine world, farmers grew olives and grapes on the stony hills and built their homes, churches, baths and presses of fine dressed stone. When trade routes shifted and the Arab conquests came, the villages emptied, but the buildings were so solid that they remained, roofless but recognisable. The best of them, grouped into a number of parks, were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2011 as the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria.

Kafr Nabo is one of them, and it holds a surprise: a temple of an older faith that was later turned into a church, a reminder that these hills were pagan before they were Christian. Near it the great church of Saint Simeon, built in the fifth century around the pillar on which the ascetic Simeon the Stylite spent decades of his life, was once the largest church in the world. Pilgrims came from across the Mediterranean to see him, and the ruin, with its four basilicas around a central octagon, is among the finest early Christian monuments anywhere.

The Jebel Sem'an lies in a part of Syria that has seen heavy fighting in recent years, the monuments suffered damage, and the region has been closed to most visitors. Official travel advice from nearly every country advises against any visit. The nearest towns, Nubl and Afrin, are both sizeable, but conditions on the ground are unpredictable.

What can be said is how the landscape looks in peaceful times. The hills are rocky and pale, scattered with olive trees, dry-stone walls and fields of wheat, and in spring they are green and dotted with red poppies. The air is clear, the soil is thin, and the ruins, with their arched windows and carved lintels, stand against the sky like drawings. It is a place to look forward to visiting one day, when the situation allows, and for now to read about in the work of archaeologists and travellers who knew it before.
t.kaya kinondo@-4.4,39.5:
The beaches of Diani are famous for white sand and turquoise water, and a short walk inland a forest that is older than the hotels keeps its own rules. Kaya Kinondo is the last sizeable fragment of the coastal forest that once covered the southern coast of Kenya, and for the Digo people it is a sacred grove, the place where their ancestors settled and where the elders still perform ceremonies. It is one of the Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests, inscribed in 2008, and it differs from some of the others in having a well-organised community programme, run by the Digo elders, which lets visitors in with a guide.

The rules are part of the experience. Visitors are asked to leave shoes, bags and cameras at the entrance, women are asked to wear a traditional wrap over their trousers or shorts, and everyone follows the elder along a narrow path. Inside, the forest is dark, cool and quiet, with tall trees, lianas and a rich growth of mosses, and you are told which trees are used as medicine and which are sacred. The forest is home to black-and-white colobus monkeys, bush babies, butterflies and rare plants, and the Diani coast is one of the few places where the Angolan colobus is still common.

Reaching the kaya is a good coastal ride. From Mombasa you cross the Likoni ferry, a crowded, noisy, but efficient service that carries vehicles and thousands of walking passengers across the harbour channel, and then follow the main road south through palm groves, baobabs and small markets. The road is busy with trucks, buses and tuk-tuks, so ride with full attention, and avoid riding after dark, when pedestrians and animals are hard to see. The coast is hot and humid all year, with a rainy period in April and May, and the cooler dry months from June to October are most pleasant.

Gazi and Sawa Sawa are small towns on the coast, and Ukunda, near Diani Beach, has petrol stations, shops, restaurants and cash machines. The coast's Swahili cooking, with coconut rice, grilled fish, and sweet, spicy tea, is a pleasure after a day on the road.
t.lake nakuru@-0.4,36.1:
The first thing you notice about Lake Nakuru is the smell, and the second is the pink. The lake sits in the floor of the Great Rift Valley about 1,760 metres above sea level with no outlet, so the water is soda-rich, alkaline and rank, and in a good year it is thick with blue-green algae that lesser flamingos feed on in the hundreds of thousands. From the ridge above the shoreline they look like a pink smudge across the grey water. In other years, when the water level changes, the birds move to Lake Bogoria or Elmenteita, which is why the trio of Rift Valley soda lakes is listed together as a World Heritage site.

The national park around the lake is small but well stocked: white rhino, black rhino, Rothschild's giraffe, buffalo, waterbuck and the occasional leopard in the yellow-barked acacia woodland, with euphorbia trees spread like candelabras on the hillsides. Baboon Cliff, a rocky outcrop above the water, gives the best overview. Over the last decade the lake rose dramatically and swallowed shoreline roads and some park buildings, which is a useful reminder that the Rift's lakes breathe in and out with the rains.

For a motorcyclist the park itself is the awkward part. Kenyan national parks generally do not welcome bikes inside, because of the animals, so check the rules at the gate and expect to leave the bike outside or join a vehicle tour. The ride to get here is the reward. The A104 from Nairobi climbs through highland farms and tea country, then drops off the escarpment with a huge view of the Rift Valley opening out, before running along the valley floor past Lake Naivasha. Expect trucks, matatu minibuses driving like they are in a hurry, speed bumps in every village and police checkpoints; the tarmac is generally decent but can break up at edges.

Nakuru town, a city of a quarter of a million about six kilometres from the lake, has fuel, food and every kind of repair shop. Nights are cool at this altitude and mornings can be cold. The best time is the dry season, from January to February or June to September, when the roads are clear and animals gather near water.

Take a jacket for dawn, sunscreen for noon, and binoculars always.
t.karain site@38.6,35.0:
Cappadocia is a land that was made by volcanoes and then carved by people. Millions of years ago, the eruptions of Mount Erciyes, which still stands at 3,917 metres, and other volcanoes covered the high plateau of central Anatolia with deep layers of ash, which hardened into a soft rock called tuff. Wind and water then eroded the tuff into valleys of pinnacles, cones and ridges, the fairy chimneys, and people found that the rock was easy to dig. Ever since, they have been carving houses, churches, stables and storerooms into it.

Karain, near Ürgüp, belongs to that landscape, and the label points to the rock-cut world that lies all around. In the early centuries of Christianity, communities of monks settled in the valleys of Cappadocia and decorated rock chapels with frescoes of saints and Bible stories, some still vivid with red and blue. The Göreme Open Air Museum is the best known, and many other churches are scattered across the valleys, often reached by narrow paths. Beneath the plateau, the underground cities of Kaymaklı and Derinkuyu run down for many levels, with storerooms, wells and stone doors that rolled across the passages in case of attack.

The ride in Cappadocia is gentle and spacious. The roads are generally good, running through high, treeless country of vineyards, apricot orchards and fields, with pale rock formations rising on either side. Dawn brings hot-air balloons, dozens of them drifting over the valleys, and the roads fill with tour vans heading to viewpoints. Traffic around Göreme and Uçhisar can be heavy in summer, so go early. In winter the plateau is cold, with snow and ice, and the fairy chimneys look magical under frost.

Ürgüp, a town of sixteen thousand, has fuel, shops and wine bars. Cappadocia has a long tradition of winemaking, and local reds and whites are a pleasure after a day's ride. Pottery from nearby Avanos, shaped from the red clay of the Kızılırmak river, is worth a look, and a meal of testi kebab, cooked in a sealed clay pot that is broken open at the table, is a local spectacle.

Visit in spring or autumn, when the temperature is mild and the light is soft.
t.jebel sem an 1 qal atsem an@36.3,36.8:
Saint Simeon the Stylite spent more than three decades on top of a pillar, and the ruins of the great church built around that pillar still stand in the limestone hills northwest of Aleppo. Simeon, a fifth-century monk from the region, withdrew from the world by climbing onto a column that was raised gradually to about eighteen metres, and from there he preached, prayed and advised pilgrims until his death in 459. Pilgrims came from across the Byzantine world, and within a few decades, a vast cruciform church, one of the largest of its time, rose around the base of the pillar.

Qal'at Sem'an, the fortress of Simeon, is the name given to the ruins. They include four basilicas arranged in a cross around an octagonal courtyard, with the stump of the pillar at its centre, and richly carved arches and capitals that rank among the finest examples of early Byzantine architecture. The location is on the Jebel Sem'an, a limestone massif dotted with the ruins of ancient villages, houses, churches and tombs, known as the Dead Cities, which were abandoned from the seventh century onwards and are astonishingly well preserved.

The area has been affected by years of war, and the monument was damaged in 2016 during fighting. Historically, the ride into the hills was a quiet one, along narrow roads through olive groves and stone walls, with fields of wheat and bare limestone in the sun.

Practical knowledge from before the conflict suggests that Aleppo, about thirty kilometres away, was the usual base, with fuel and services in the city. Smaller towns such as Nubl, a larger place at some distance, have a few shops. Summer is hot and dry, winter is cool and wet, and spring is the most pleasant, with wildflowers on the limestone.

If you are reading this for history alone, the site's story of a man on a pillar is worth remembering.
t.gobekli tepe@37.2,38.9:
Göbekli Tepe turned the story of civilisation upside down. On a limestone ridge above the plain north-east of Şanlıurfa, about thirteen kilometres from the city, hunter-gatherers raised rings of enormous T-shaped stone pillars more than eleven thousand years ago, some of them taller than a bus and carved with foxes, snakes, boars, vultures and scorpions. That is some six thousand years before Stonehenge, and before pottery, metal tools or farming had been invented. The assumption had been that people built monuments after they settled and farmed. Göbekli Tepe suggests that the urge to gather and build may have come first.

The German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began to dig the site in the mid-1990s, after surveying a hill that others had written off as a medieval cemetery, and work has gone on ever since. Only a fraction of the mound has been excavated, and geophysical surveys show many more enclosures beneath the soil. Nobody knows for certain what the circles were for, whether temples, meeting places or something else, and that uncertainty is part of the fascination. A walkway and a modern canopy now protect the main enclosures, and the visitor centre explains the finds. The site was listed by UNESCO in 2018.

Şanlıurfa itself deserves time. Known locally as Urfa, and in antiquity as Edessa, it is a city of golden stone, with a pool of sacred carp beside the mosques at Balıklıgöl where tradition places the birthplace of Abraham, and a bazaar of copper workers and spice sellers. Its cooking is among the best in Turkey: Urfa kebab, mildly spiced and served with onion and sumac, lahmacun, and the dark flaked pepper called isot, which tastes of smoke and raisins.

The ride from the city is short, across a dry plain of wheat, cotton and pistachio. Roads are good, traffic is moderate and the summer heat is formidable, often over forty degrees, which makes midday on the exposed hilltop a trial. The cooler months of spring and autumn are better, though winters can be wet and cold. Fuel is easy in Şanlıurfa, a city of nearly half a million, and the site has a café and parking.

Go early, carry water and wear a hat, because the ridge offers almost no shade.
t.nemrut dag@38.0,38.7:
Nemrut Dağ is a mountain with a king on top. In the first century BC, Antiochus I of Commagene, ruler of a small kingdom between the Roman and Parthian empires, ordered a tomb-sanctuary built on a summit 2,134 metres high, and had it crowned with a tumulus of crushed stone about fifty metres high. On terraces to the east and west sat colossal limestone statues, perhaps eight to nine metres tall, of himself, gods who mixed Greek and Persian traditions, and guardian lions and eagles. Earthquakes and time have toppled the heads, which now lie in rows on the ground, staring out at the mountains.

Antiochus claimed descent from both Alexander the Great and the kings of Persia, and the sanctuary expresses that mixture of East and West. Inscriptions on the terraces describe his intentions and the rituals for his cult. Nowhere else does a small kingdom's ambition feel so large. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage property since 1987, and sunrise and sunset are the most popular times to visit, when the heads glow in the low light and the range of the Taurus mountains fades into layers of blue.

Getting there is half the pleasure. The approach from Sincik or Kahta climbs through a hard, bare landscape of rock and scrub, and the last section to the summit car park is steep, with hairpins. Part of the way up can be rough, and the final stretch to the terraces is on foot over loose stones. The mountain is high enough that snow lies across the road from late autumn until spring, and the summit is generally accessible only from about May to October. Wind at the top is cold even in July, so carry a jacket.

Fuel is available in Kahta and Adıyaman, the nearest larger towns, and Sincik has a small selection. On the way, look for the Roman bridge at Cendere, built in the second century with a pair of columns for each emperor, and the burial mounds at Karakuş and Arsameia. Small guesthouses near the summit cater for those who want to see both sunset and sunrise.

Plan your summit visit around the weather and expect crowds at dawn in high summer.
t.ngorongoro conservation area@-3.2,35.5:
Ngorongoro is a volcano that fell in on itself. Millions of years ago, a mountain as high as Kilimanjaro erupted and collapsed, leaving a caldera about twenty kilometres across, whose floor is some six hundred metres below the rim, and it is one of the largest unbroken calderas in the world. The crater floor holds grassland, a soda lake, springs and a patch of fever-tree forest, and it supports around twenty-five thousand large animals, including wildebeest, zebra, lions, hyenas, elephants, buffalo and some of the last black rhino in East Africa.

The conservation area around the crater is a living landscape. Maasai pastoralists graze their cattle, sheep and goats on the highlands, as they have for generations, and you will see herders in red cloaks beside the roads. To the north-west, Olduvai Gorge is where Mary and Louis Leakey found early human fossils, and at Laetoli, further south, a trail of footprints left by human ancestors some three and a half million years ago was preserved in volcanic ash. UNESCO has listed the area for both its nature and its human story.

The approach from Arusha is a long ride through farmland and the town of Karatu to the park gate, with good tarmac and a steady climb to the rim at over 2,200 metres. The air at the rim is cold, and mist and cloud are common, so bring warm clothes and a waterproof. The road along the rim is gravel, with a few hairpins, and a descent into the crater is made by a steep track that is generally limited to four-wheel-drive vehicles with a ranger. Check in advance whether motorcycles are permitted in the conservation area, as rules may restrict them, and expect to pay fees at the gate.

Fuel is available at Karatu and Arusha, and there is little beyond the gate, so fill up before you ascend. Lodges on the rim offer meals and rooms with views across the crater.

The dry months from June to October give the best wildlife viewing and the most reliable roads.
t.pereslavl zalessky@56.7,38.9:
Pereslavl-Zalessky lies on the shore of a lake that Peter the Great used as a toy box, and the toy box included real ships. As a teenager, around 1688, the future emperor built a small fleet on Lake Pleshcheyevo, and the surviving boat, the Fortuna, along with some later models, can be seen in the Botik museum on the lakeside. The town is about a hundred and thirty kilometres north-east of Moscow, one of the old towns of the Golden Ring, and the lake itself is a broad sheet of water ringed by low wooded hills and fishing villages.

The history is deeper than Peter's play. The town was founded in the twelfth century by Yuri Dolgoruky, the same prince who is credited with founding Moscow, and Alexander Nevsky, the prince who defeated the Swedes and Teutonic knights in the thirteenth century, was born here in 1220. The white stone Transfiguration Cathedral of the 1150s, rising from the old earth ramparts in the centre of town, is among the oldest surviving buildings in north-eastern Russia, with plain, powerful walls and a single dome. Around the town stand several old monasteries, including Goritsky and Nikitsky, with brick walls and golden domes reflected in ponds. Local fishermen smoke small lake fish called ryapushka, a regional speciality sold at roadside stalls.

For riders, the backroads north toward Yuryev-Polsky and Suzdal run through quiet Russian countryside, with fields of rye and sunflowers, birch groves, wooden villages and small churches on the hills. The surface varies from smooth asphalt to broken patches, with potholes after the winter, and trucks and tractors share the road. The best times are late spring and early autumn, when birches turn yellow, and summer can be hot with sudden storms. Mosquitoes are common near the water, especially at dusk.

Pereslavl has fuel stations, shops and cafés, and small guesthouses by the lake. The town is popular with Muscovites at weekends, so the roads and restaurants are busier then. A morning walk along the earth ramparts before the crowds arrive, with mist rising off the lake, shows the town at its most atmospheric.
t.mombasa@-4.0,39.7:
Mombasa is an island, and that single fact explains its history. A small coral island lies between two inlets on Kenya's coast, joined to the mainland by causeways and a bridge, with a deep natural harbour that made it one of the great ports of the Indian Ocean. Arab, Persian, Indian and Portuguese traders came here for centuries, bringing cloth, spices and slaves and leaving behind a coastal Swahili culture that mixes African and Arab elements.

Fort Jesus, built by the Portuguese between 1593 and 1596, squats at the harbour mouth, its thick coral-stone walls a reminder of the fierce competition for the coast. Control passed between the Portuguese and the Omani Arabs for a century, and the fort changed hands many times. It is now a museum and World Heritage site. The old town around it has narrow lanes, carved wooden doors, balconies and mosques, with a hot, salty smell of spices, fish and diesel. Tusk-shaped arches on Moi Avenue mark the main street.

The riding is hot, humid and lively. Traffic is dense, with matatus, tuk-tuks, lorries from the port and motorcycle taxis, so confidence and patience help. Roads outside the island lead north toward Malindi and Kilifi, through coconut palms and baobab trees, with sea views and fishing villages, and south toward Diani Beach after the Likoni ferry. The surface can be rough, with potholes. The hottest months are February and March, and the long rains come in April and May.

Fuel is available all over Mombasa and along the main roads. Food is a joy: coconut-rich fish curries, biryani, mahamri, a spiced fried bread, and nyama choma, grilled meat. Fresh coconut water and sugar-cane juice are sold by the roadside. Kaya Jibana, one of the sacred forests of the Mijikenda people, lies in the hinterland, and the kayas are protected as World Heritage for the way communities have kept their spiritual forests. Ask permission and a local guide, and respect local customs.
t.tver@56.9,35.9:
Tver is the city that nearly became Moscow. In the fourteenth century its princes were Moscow's great rivals, and the two fought for the right to rule the Russian lands, until Moscow won and Tver was absorbed in 1485. Mikhail of Tver, who was killed by the Mongol Golden Horde, was later made a saint. What remains is a river city on the upper Volga, at the point where the Tvertsa joins it, roughly halfway between Moscow and St Petersburg, which made it a natural stop for anyone travelling between the two capitals.

That role gave it a place in the history of the road. The route between Moscow and St Petersburg ran through Tver, and in the eighteenth century Catherine the Great ordered the city rebuilt after a great fire in 1763. The result is a neat classical centre of radial streets and pastel buildings, including the Imperial Travel Palace, built so the royal family had somewhere to stay on the way. The Tver merchant Afanasy Nikitin, who travelled to India in the fifteenth century and wrote of it, is remembered with a statue on the Volga embankment. The Volga here is still young, wide and calm, with willows on the banks.

Riders heading from Solnechnogorsk up to Tver are following an old royal road, and the route is mostly fast, with a busy modern highway running alongside and smaller roads that wander through villages with wooden houses and onion-domed churches. Surfaces vary, and trucks are heavy on the main road, so take care in the rain. The best season is late spring to early autumn, with the forests at their best in September.

Tver has some four hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and hotels are easy to find, and the villages around it, such as Sakharovo, have basics. Look for a cafe on the embankment, where you can watch the river traffic. Foreign riders should check current conditions and requirements before planning travel in Russia.
t.yaroslavl@57.6,39.9:
Yaroslavl stands on the Volga at the mouth of the Kotorosl, and its old centre is the best preserved in the Golden Ring. According to tradition, the town was founded in 1010 by Prince Yaroslav the Wise, who, the story goes, killed a bear on the spot, which is why a bear is on the city's coat of arms to this day. UNESCO added the historic centre to the World Heritage list in 2005, mostly for its churches, which date mainly from the seventeenth century, when the city grew rich on trade along the Volga.

The churches are the thing to see. The Church of Elijah the Prophet, built in the 1650s, has frescoes covering every wall, painted in bright blues, reds and golds, and its five domes are among the prettiest in Russia. The Spaso-Preobrazhensky Monastery, a fortified complex with a bell tower that gives a wide view over the river, is just next to it. At the Strelka, the point where the two rivers meet, a park runs down to the water, and in the evening locals walk and watch boats pass. The Volkov Theatre, founded here in 1750, is claimed as the first professional theatre in Russia.

The roads here are flat, with broad views over fields and forest. The highway to Moscow, the M8, is fast and heavy, with trucks, while the smaller roads to Kostroma and Rostov run through villages with wooden houses and gardens full of sunflowers and hollyhocks. Surfaces are mixed, with patches of poor asphalt, and in spring after the thaw, potholes can be bad. The best time is late summer and early autumn, when the light is soft and the fields are golden.

With over six hundred thousand people, Yaroslavl has all the fuel, food and repairs a rider could need, and the smaller towns around it, like Tunoshna, add a few more. Parking is easy near the centre, though the cobbled streets are rough on a bike. Foreign riders should check what is currently possible before planning travel.
t.uglich@57.5,38.3:
A boy died in Uglich in 1591, and the history of Russia changed. Tsarevich Dmitry, the youngest son of Ivan the Terrible, was found with his throat cut in the courtyard of the town's kremlin, and whether it was murder or an accident has been argued ever since. His death left the throne without an heir, set off the Time of Troubles, and gave rise to a string of pretenders who claimed to be the lost prince. The Church of St Dmitry on the Blood, a red-and-white building with blue domes on the spot, is one of the town's best-known sights.

Uglich is a small town on the upper Volga with a lot of charm. The river was dammed here in 1940, so the water is now a broad reservoir, and the old centre sits above it with churches, merchants' houses and a monastery on the bank. The town's bell is a local legend: it rang to signal the death of the tsarevich, and as a punishment it was whipped, had its tongue removed, and was exiled to Siberia, only returning in 1892. Uglich also makes cheese, which is sold in the market, and a plate of it with local honey is a good lunch.

The riding around is gentle and green. Roads to Myshkin, about thirty kilometres away, wind through villages and meadows, and Myshkin itself is a small town known for its mouse museum and its quiet streets. To the west, the huge Rybinsk Reservoir spreads out like a sea, with flooded forests and migrating birds. Surfaces range from fair to rough, and traffic is light, though trucks use the main roads. Summer is the best season, with long evenings and clear skies.

Uglich has about thirty-eight thousand people, so fuel, food and rooms are easy to find. Myshkin is smaller, so top up here first. Walk along the embankment in the evening, when the light on the water is lovely. Foreign riders should check current conditions and rules before planning a trip.
t.zvenigorod@55.7,36.9:
Zvenigorod is one of the old towns of the Moscow region, set on a high bluff above the Moskva River about fifty kilometres west of the capital, and it has long been a favourite place for city people to escape to. Its Russian nickname, the Russian Switzerland, is generous, but the wooded hills, the river bends and the onion domes among the birches do make a gentle, harmonious landscape. About sixteen thousand people live here today, and the place has fuel, shops, cafés and a quiet, provincial air.

The town's story begins in the fourteenth century, when it was the seat of a princely appanage, and a fortress stood on the hill called Gorodok. The Dormition Cathedral there, built around 1399, is one of the oldest surviving stone churches in the region and contains remnants of medieval frescoes attributed to the school of Andrei Rublev. A few kilometres away, the Savvino-Storozhevsky Monastery, founded in 1398 by the monk Savva at the invitation of Prince Yuri, is a handsome walled complex with white-stone churches, bright towers and a long role in the history of Russia's tsars, who favoured it as a retreat.

In the nineteenth century, Zvenigorod became a summer resort, and artists and writers came to stay. The painter Isaac Levitan worked here in the 1880s and left landscapes that made the hills famous, and Anton Chekhov served as a district doctor in 1884 and 1885, treating local people while he wrote. Their names are still tied to the town, with memorial museums and walks.

For a rider, the roads in the area are gentle and scenic, with smooth country lanes winding through birch forest and meadow, fields of rye and small villages with wooden houses. Mozhaisk Highway is busy, particularly at weekends when Muscovites head for their dachas, so go early. Summer is warm and green, autumn is golden, and winter is cold and snowy, and the surface can be icy. Fill up before you go, enjoy a plate of pelmeni or a bowl of soup in a café, and walk the monastery walls in the evening.
t.lake manyara@-3.5,35.8:
The Great Rift Valley has a wall, and at Lake Manyara it stands about six hundred metres high, a green escarpment rising behind the shallow soda lake like the side of a great bowl. The lake is alkaline and shallow, and its edges are fringed with groundwater forest, where giant mahogany and fig trees shade a floor of tall grass. Elephants, buffalo, giraffe and baboons use the forest, and flamingos, pelicans and other water birds gather on the water in vast numbers when conditions are right. The park is also famous for its tree-climbing lions, which lounge on the branches of acacia trees, a habit that is rare elsewhere.

Ernest Hemingway is said to have called Manyara the loveliest lake he had seen in Africa, and on a clear morning, with the mist lifting off the water and the escarpment glowing in the sun, it is easy to agree. The nearest town, Mto wa Mbu, whose name means river of mosquitoes in Swahili, is a lively and colourful place, with a market, banana plantations and a patchwork of people from across Tanzania, selling fruit, carvings and cloth along the main road.

The road to the north, part of the route from Arusha to Ngorongoro, is mostly fast and well surfaced, until it reaches the escarpment, where it climbs in tight bends through forest and farmland to the highlands. Trucks, buses and minibuses are everywhere, and overtaking is ambitious, so stay alert. Cattle and goats wander onto the road, and herders from the Maasai communities walk beside it with their flocks. Motorbikes are not allowed in national parks, so the park itself is for safari vehicles, but the road around is yours.

Fuel is available in Mto wa Mbu and at Karatu, up on the highlands, and it is a good idea to fill the tank before climbing. The weather is hot in the valley and noticeably cooler on the highlands, so dress in layers. The dry season, from June to October, is best for game viewing, and the rains of March to May turn the track to mud. At dusk, the sound of frogs and insects rises from the lake, and the sunset glows red over the water.
t.olduvai gorge@-3.0,35.4:
Olduvai Gorge is a scar across the dry plains of northern Tanzania, about forty-eight kilometres long and nearly a hundred metres deep, and what it holds is nothing less than the story of our own beginnings. The walls of the gorge expose layers of volcanic ash and sediment laid down over almost two million years, and in them Louis and Mary Leakey, working over decades, found stone tools and the bones of early humans. In 1959 Mary Leakey uncovered a skull of an early hominin, now called Paranthropus boisei, and later work produced remains of Homo habilis, one of the first members of our own genus.

A few dozen kilometres to the south lie the Laetoli footprints, a trail of tracks left in volcanic ash more than three million years ago by early human ancestors walking upright, one of the most moving finds in all of archaeology. At Olduvai itself, a small museum on the rim displays fossils and tools and explains the work, and guides take visitors down to the spots where key finds were made. The name comes from the Maasai word for the wild sisal that grows in the gorge.

The landscape around is open, dry and wide, a golden savanna of grass and flat-topped acacias. Maasai herders move with their cattle across the plain, and wildlife, including wildebeest, zebra and gazelles, appears at certain times of year. The road runs between the Ngorongoro crater highlands and the Serengeti plains, and the temperature swings from cool mornings to hot afternoons. The surface is a mixture of paved and gravel sections, with dust and corrugations on the unpaved parts, and heavy safari vehicles that throw up clouds. Check whether motorcycles are permitted in the conservation area, because restrictions apply and fees are charged.

The midday sun is fierce, with little shade, so bring a hat and sunscreen. The best months for visiting are from June to October, when the weather is dry and clear. At sunset, the walls of the gorge turn orange and red, a fitting colour for the oldest chapter of the human story.
t.kayseri@38.7,35.5:
Mount Erciyes dominates Kayseri in a way that the city seems to accept without comment. The extinct volcano rises to about 3,900 metres above the plain, snow-capped for much of the year, and its cone is visible from almost every street. Kayseri sits at its foot, a big, practical, trading city of nearly 600,000 with a black basalt citadel in the middle that was rebuilt by the Seljuks in the thirteenth century. The Seljuks left their mark here in the form of tomb towers, mosques and a medical school, the Gevher Nesibe complex, from 1206, which was one of the first of its kind.

Kayseri was called Caesarea in Roman times, and the surrounding area has even older roots. A few kilometres to the north-east, the mound of Kültepe held an Assyrian trading colony four thousand years ago, where merchants kept records on clay tablets, some of the oldest business letters in the world. The great architect Sinan, who designed many of the best Ottoman buildings in Istanbul, was born in a village nearby.

Riding out of the city, the landscape opens into the high steppe of central Anatolia: wide, almost treeless, with fields of wheat and sugar beet and volcanic hills. Roads are generally good, often very straight, with wind as the main hazard. Heading west and south you approach the Cappadocia region, where volcanic ash has been carved by erosion into pinnacles and valleys. The loop through the region takes in some excellent tarmac, but it is exposed, so watch the weather, especially in winter when snow can arrive early and linger.

Kayseri is also a city that likes its food. Mantı, tiny dumplings served with yoghurt and spice, is the local dish, and pastırma, a spiced air-dried beef, hangs in shop windows throughout the old town. Sucuk, the garlicky sausage, is another speciality. You will find fuel, workshops and hotels easily, and the bazaar near the citadel is a good place for a tea and a walk. May to October is the best season, and mornings are crisp even in summer.
t.arusha@-3.4,36.7:
Mount Meru gives Arusha a backdrop that most cities would envy. The volcano rises to about 4,500 metres directly behind the town, a jagged crater rim you see on clear mornings and lose in cloud by afternoon, while Kilimanjaro floats above the horizon to the east. Arusha itself sits at around 1,400 metres on fertile volcanic soil, with coffee farms, banana groves and flower plantations on the surrounding slopes. It is a busy, dusty, friendly town of more than 300,000 people, the gateway for safaris to the northern parks, and the place where the Arusha Declaration of 1967 laid out Tanzania's socialist policies under Julius Nyerere. The Maasai are a constant presence, in their red shuka cloths, selling beads and herding cattle on the edge of town.

Leaving Arusha westward, the road, the A104, runs across a plain, past the Maasai steppe, and then climbs the wall of the Rift Valley near Lake Manyara. The road is generally good tarmac, but trucks and buses are heavy, and Tanzanian drivers take risks on blind curves, so patience matters. From the escarpment, the view over the lake and the rift floor is huge, and the colour of the light changes by the hour.

A very important note concerns the national parks. Tanzania charges substantial fees to enter Ngorongoro and Serengeti, and the rules for motorbikes in those areas are strict, as riding in wildlife areas is generally not allowed for visitors. Anyone planning this route should check with park authorities and tour operators well ahead, because a trip may need to be done in a vehicle with a guide. Dangerous animals, including lions, buffalo and elephants, are real, and not something to meet on a motorcycle.

Fuel, supplies and repair shops are plentiful in Arusha, so fill the tank, check the bike and buy water before leaving. Try nyama choma, grilled meat with kachumbari salad, at a local bar, and Kilimanjaro or Safari beer. The dry seasons, June to October and January to February, are best, while April and May bring heavy rain that turns dirt roads to mud.
t.ponte vedra beach@30.2,-81.4:
The beach at Ponte Vedra is a wide band of pale sand that drops gently into the Atlantic, backed by dunes with sea oats and low scrub, and the coast road behind it, State Road A1A, runs for miles in a sequence of palm trees, big houses and glimpses of the water. It is an affluent place now, with golf courses, tennis clubs and gated communities, and home to the headquarters of the PGA Tour and the TPC Sawgrass course, where the Players Championship is played each year and the par-three seventeenth hole sits on an island green that has humbled the best golfers in the world.

The name sounds Spanish but was made up in the early twentieth century, and the area was first developed not for golf but for mining. Prospectors found that the beach sands here held titanium-bearing minerals such as rutile and ilmenite, used in paint and later in the war effort, and for a time the community was called Mineral City. The mining stopped, and the town turned to tourism, which proved far more lasting.

On a motorcycle, A1A is a relaxed run rather than a technical one. The road follows the barrier island south toward St. Augustine, the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the United States, established by the Spanish in 1565, with a stone fort and narrow streets worth a long stop. Northward, the route leads to the Mayport ferry and the beaches of Jacksonville. The surface is generally good, with long straight sections broken by gentle bends, bridges across tidal creeks and marsh, and low sunlight through the palms. Speed limits are enforced, and summer traffic can be heavy near beaches.

Weather deserves attention. Thunderstorms arrive suddenly on summer afternoons with lightning and heavy rain, and hurricane season runs from June to November. Winter days are mild, with morning chill sometimes dipping near freezing in January. For fuel and food, the community of about thirty-five thousand people has everything, with a long list of seafood restaurants, bakeries and cafes. October to May is the best time to ride, with clear air and warm sun.
t.dmitrov@56.3,37.5:
Dmitrov is an old town north of Moscow, set above the Yakhroma River where the Moscow Canal begins its run to the Volga. It was founded in 1154 by Prince Yuri Dolgoruky, the same prince credited with founding Moscow, and named for his son Dmitry, and its earthen ramparts, the remains of a medieval fortress called the Kremlin, still encircle a hill in the middle of town. Inside stands the white Assumption Cathedral, a sixteenth-century church with a wide dome, a calm landmark above the lower streets.

The canal is the other half of the story. The Moscow-Volga Canal was dug in the 1930s, largely by prisoners of the Gulag, with Dmitrov as the headquarters of the building administration, and it opened in 1937. The waterway runs north from here past locks, pumping stations and monumental stone portals, and its grim history sits oddly with the calm water and pleasure boats of today. The anarchist thinker Peter Kropotkin lived out his last years in Dmitrov, and his house is now a small museum, a quiet footnote to the town's story.

For riders, Dmitrov is a gateway to the quiet country north of the capital. The roads east and west of the canal pass through low, rolling farmland, birch woods and small villages with wooden houses, and the Klin-Dmitrov Ridge, the highest ground in the Moscow region, rises to the west. The surface in the district varies, with good main roads and rougher secondary ones, and potholes after the winter thaw can be deep. The countryside is gentle, and the pace is slow, with plenty of stops for a roadside samovar or a cup of tea.

Dmitrov is a town of sixty thousand, so fuel, food and shops are plentiful, and the road to Moscow is fast. Yakhroma, a few kilometers north, has a large textile factory and a canal viewing point. The best time is late spring, when the birches are in leaf, and September, when the woods turn gold, but July can be hot and the roads busy with city dwellers heading for dachas. Winter brings deep snow and hard frost, and the roads, though plowed, are slick and cold, so it is a season for the brave.
t.mozhaysk@55.5,36.0:
Mozhaysk is the town on the road to Borodino, and Borodino is the reason most people know it. On 7 September 1812, about a dozen kilometers west of here, Napoleon's Grande Armée fought Kutuzov's Russian army in the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars, with tens of thousands killed or wounded in a few hours. The battlefield is now a vast open-air museum, with monuments, restored earthworks like the Raevsky Battery, and a landscape of wide fields and birch groves that is moving in its quiet.

Mozhaysk itself is an old town, first recorded in the twelfth century, with a hilltop kremlin of earthen ramparts and a white-stone cathedral. A famous medieval statue of St Nicholas of Mozhaysk, a wooden figure holding a sword in one hand and a city in the other, is the town's emblem and appears on its coat of arms. The Luzhetsky Monastery, founded in the fifteenth century, sits on the riverbank below. After the battle, the town was crowded with wounded, and the churches were turned into hospitals.

Near the battlefield, the Spaso-Borodinsky Convent was founded by Margarita Tuchkova, a general's widow who lost her husband at Borodino and built a church to his memory, a poignant and well-kept place. The road from Mozhaysk to Borodino follows the old Smolensk highway, the same route Napoleon took toward Moscow, and the open, rolling landscape lets you picture the armies. Riding is straightforward, on mostly decent surfaces, with gentle bends past fields and villages.

Mozhaysk has fuel, a market, shops and cafes, with the highway to Moscow a fast run of about a hundred kilometers. The reservoir to the north, a large, quiet lake, offers fishing and picnicking in summer. The best months are May to September, with early autumn the most comfortable, and the anniversary of the battle in early September draws reenactors in period uniform to the field. Winters are long and snowy, and spring brings mud, so avoid the unpaved side roads then. The M1 highway is busy, so leave early on weekends to avoid the dacha traffic.
t.helen@34.7,-83.7:
Helen is a Bavarian village in the Georgia mountains, an improbable idea that somehow works. Founded as a lumber town in the early twentieth century, it fell on hard times after the timber ran out, and in the late 1960s local businessmen, looking for a way to attract tourists, hired an artist to redesign the town in the style of an Alpine village. Today, half-timbered buildings with painted facades, flower boxes, cobbled alleys and signs in German script line the streets, and the Oktoberfest, held from mid-September through October, is among the longest in the country.

The setting is real. The Chattahoochee River, which begins in the hills a short way north, runs through the middle of town at an altitude of about 430 meters, and in summer crowds float down it on inner tubes. Nearby, Anna Ruby Falls drops in twin cascades from the slopes of Tray Mountain, and Unicoi State Park offers a lake and trails. The surrounding hills of the Chattahoochee National Forest are steep and wooded, with oak, hickory and rhododendron, and the southern Appalachians' blue haze hangs over everything.

For riders, Helen is the start of the Richard B. Russell Scenic Highway, Georgia 348, a short, twisting mountain road that climbs over Hogpen Gap, at roughly 3,400 feet, crossing the Appalachian Trail on its way to the Vogel State Park area. The road has tight curves, steep grades and glimpses of long ridges, and it is well maintained, with light traffic outside weekends. Georgia 75 and Georgia 180, the Wolf Pen Gap road, are other good routes, and the notorious Tail of the Dragon in North Carolina is not far away.

The village has fuel, restaurants and parking that fills on weekends, and Cleveland, a short ride south, has larger supermarkets and stations. The best months are April and May, when the dogwoods bloom, and October, though Oktoberfest brings traffic jams that can last for hours on peak weekends. Summer is hot and humid, and afternoon thunderstorms are common. Winter can bring ice on the high gaps. Watch for gravel, wet leaves and other riders pushing too hard on the bends.
t.wolf pen gap@34.8,-83.9:
Wolf Pen Gap is a notch in the Blue Ridge of north Georgia, and the road that goes through it is a favourite of southern motorcyclists, with good reason. Georgia 348, the Richard B. Russell Scenic Highway, climbs out of the valley of the Chattahoochee watershed in a tight series of bends, shaded by hardwoods and rhododendron, then drops down the other side toward Suches. At around 900 metres, the gap is not high by western standards, but the road feels a lot more serious than the number, because the curves come quickly, one after another, with little straight in between.

The highway is named for a long-serving senator from Georgia, and it forms part of a scenic byway through the Chattahoochee National Forest, which spreads for hundreds of thousands of acres across the southern Appalachians. The forest is rich: oak, hickory, tulip poplar, hemlock and white pine, with laurel thickets, mountain streams and, in spring, flowering dogwood. Black bears live here, as do white-tailed deer, so dawn and dusk need care. Fall colour peaks in October, and the whole range turns a patchwork of reds and golds.

On the road, take it carefully. The bends are tight, some are blind, and the surface can be damp and leaf-strewn, with gravel washed onto the apex after rain. In the warm months, the road draws plenty of other riders, and a few sections have been the scene of crashes, so traffic can be unpredictable. Cars cut corners, and so do bikes, so keep to your side and take the line you would be happy to be seen taking. Early morning on a weekday, when there is mist in the hollows and no one about, is the best time.

The area has history, too. In 1828, gold was found near Dahlonega, setting off the first major gold rush in the United States, years before California. The Cherokee had lived in these mountains for centuries before they were forced out in the 1830s on the Trail of Tears, and their story is part of the landscape. Dahlonega, with its town square, gold museum and wine tasting rooms, is a good place to spend a quiet hour.

Services are scarce up here. Suches has a little community and a small store, but do not rely on fuel on the mountain. Blairsville, around twelve kilometres away, and Dahlonega, twenty-six, have proper stations, so fill up in one of them. Cell signal drops out in the hollows, so carry a map.
t.blairsville@34.9,-84.0:
Blairsville is a small mountain town, the seat of Union County, and it sits in a bowl of the north Georgia hills at about 570 meters, in country that Georgians think of as the high mountains. The town square has an old courthouse and a few shops, and the surrounding roads lead to some of the best scenery in the state. In October the town holds the Sorghum Festival, a local tradition with syrup-making, music and crafts that draws crowds from across the region.

The hills around are a point of pride. Brasstown Bald, the highest point in Georgia at 4,784 feet, rises a short distance to the southeast, with an observation tower on the summit and a view that reaches into four states on a clear day. Vogel State Park, one of the oldest in Georgia, was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, with a lake and stone buildings. Nearby, Neels Gap, a pass on US 19 and 129, is where the Appalachian Trail passes through a building, the stone Walasi-Yi center, now an outfitter, with hikers resting on the porch beneath Blood Mountain.

For riders, the roads here are excellent. US 129 and Georgia 180 climb through the pass, with tight bends and steep grades, and the Richard B. Russell Scenic Highway winds down to Helen from the northern end, a short, twisting road with good views. Georgia 180, around Wolf Pen Gap, is another fine, quiet ride, and Suches and Lake Winfield Scott lie to the south. The surface is generally good, but cars drift across the centerline in some bends, and gravel and wet leaves are common.

Blairsville has fuel at several stations, a supermarket, diners and a handful of motels, so it makes a handy end to a day. Young Harris, a few kilometers north, is home to a small college, and Hiawassee has a lake and fairgrounds. The best seasons are late April, with fresh green and blossoms, and mid-October, when the whole range turns gold and red. Summer can be hot, with heavy thunderstorms, and winter brings occasional ice. Deer cross the roads at dusk, so slow down toward the end of the day.
t.nairobi@-1.3,36.8:
Nairobi sits at about 1,700 metres on the edge of the Kenyan highlands, and it is the capital of East Africa in every sense: busy, noisy, hopeful and full of traffic. With nearly three million people in the city and more around it, it is a big and fast place. The name comes from a Maasai phrase meaning cool water, a reference to the stream that once ran here, and the city grew in 1899 as a railway depot on the line from Mombasa to Uganda. It is the only major capital with a national park on its edge, where lions and giraffes can be seen against a backdrop of skyscrapers.

To ride out, plan your timing. Nairobi's traffic is notorious, and the main roads leading out of the city, especially toward Naivasha and the Rift Valley, are clogged during morning and evening peaks. Matatus, the colourful minibuses, weave in and out with little warning, boda-boda motorbike taxis are everywhere, and rules are interpreted flexibly. Ride defensively, stay visible and give trucks plenty of space. The best time to leave is early on a weekend morning, before the city wakes up.

The reward is the Rift Valley escarpment, a short distance to the northwest. The road climbs out of Nairobi through the green hills around Limuru, with tea plantations and eucalyptus, and then comes to the edge of the great rift, where the land suddenly falls away into a vast plain. The view is one of the great ones in Africa, with extinct volcanoes on the horizon and the floor of the valley far below. There are viewpoints with craft stalls, and a small chapel built by Italian prisoners of war in the 1940s stands near the edge.

Fuel is plentiful in Nairobi, and since stations are thinner beyond the main towns, fill up before you go. Food is good too: nyama choma, grilled meat with ugali and kachumbari, and strong Kenyan tea and coffee. The weather is mild, with rains in March to May and October to November, so the dry months of January, February and June to September are best. Keep valuables out of sight and park carefully in the city, and the road ahead will repay you.
t.great rift valley viewpoint@-1.0,36.6:
The ground drops away. One minute you are on a busy highway, grinding through traffic on the highlands north-west of Nairobi, and the next you are on the lip of an escarpment, looking down several hundred metres into the Great Rift Valley, a vast, hazy trough that runs from here as far as the eye can see.
