On a clear morning you see the cone of Mount Longonot across the plain, an old volcano with a crater, and the pale glint of Lake Naivasha and the Mau escarpment on the far side. It is one of those views that makes you stop and be quiet for a moment.

The viewpoint is on the old road between Limuru and the valley, where curio stalls line the verge, selling carved animals, soapstone bowls, beads and baskets. Bargaining is expected, and the sellers are good-humoured, though they can be persistent. Nearby, tucked into a fold of the escarpment at Mai Mahiu, is a small church built by Italian prisoners of war in the 1940s, a surprising piece of history in the middle of Kenya, and the nearby mission station at Kijabe has been a centre for education and medicine for more than a century.

The valley itself is part of the East African Rift, one of the great fractures of the earth's crust, where the continent is slowly pulling apart. Volcanoes, hot springs, soda lakes and steep faults mark its path through Kenya, and the escarpments are the walls of the trough. It is a landscape on the move, in geological time.

The riding is a different matter. The highway from Nairobi to Uganda is one of the busiest roads in East Africa, packed with heavy lorries, buses and matatus, the minibus taxis whose drivers have their own ideas about road space. The descent from the escarpment is steep and winding, with trucks crawling down in low gear and others overtaking with more optimism than judgement. It demands full attention, so avoid riding after dark, keep your distance, and take care on the corners where oil and fuel spills are common. The old road, which runs parallel through Kijabe, is quieter and slower, and much more pleasant on a bike. Baboons sometimes sit on the walls, and cattle and pedestrians use the verge.

Limuru, about thirteen kilometres away, and Kijabe have small stations and shops, and Naivasha has plenty. Nairobi is about fifty kilometres behind. Carry some cash, a bottle of water and a layer, because the air at this altitude can be cool and the sun is strong. The best time to come is early in the morning, when the air is clear and the valley is still blue with haze.
t.naivasha@-0.7,36.4:
Naivasha is a working town on the floor of the Rift Valley, at about nineteen hundred metres, and it exists because of the lake. Lake Naivasha is a freshwater lake, a rare thing among the soda lakes of the Kenyan Rift, and its shores have been farmed, fished and fought over for a long time. Hippos graze on the lawns at night, fish eagles scream from the acacia trees, and the water is a shifting grey-green under a big sky. The surrounding land is covered in huge greenhouses that grow roses and cut flowers for Europe, which has made the town an unlikely player in the world flower trade.

The town is a place of dust, matatus and commerce, strung along the main highway, with markets, petrol stations, banks and cafes. It is a useful place, for riders and for everyone else, and one of the best places in the region for fuel, food and supplies. Roadside stalls sell fresh fruit and roasted maize, and grilled meat, nyama choma, is the standard meal, served with ugali, a stiff maize porridge, and a cold drink. The food is cheap and filling, and the service is friendly.

Natural attractions are close. Hell's Gate National Park lies a short ride to the south, a gorge of red cliffs, hot springs and wildlife where cycling and walking are allowed among zebra, buffalo and giraffe. It is said to have inspired the setting for a famous animated film, and the geothermal power station in the park supplies a good part of Kenya's electricity. Crescent Island, in the lake, is a sanctuary where visitors can walk among wildlife, and Elsamere, the former home of Joy Adamson, who wrote Born Free, is a museum on the shore. Mount Longonot, a dormant volcano with a walkable crater rim, dominates the horizon to the south-east.

The riding here is mixed. The highway is busy with trucks, and the surface can be patchy, with potholes and uneven edges, but the side roads around the lake are quiet and give a flavour of the countryside. Dust can be a problem in the dry months, and rain in the wet season can make dirt roads slick. Livestock on the road is common, so keep a modest pace. Traffic police are frequent, and carrying your documents is essential.

Naivasha has plenty of places to stay, from lakeside lodges to basic guesthouses, and it is a natural overnight stop between Nairobi and the western highlands. The evenings are cool and the sky is brilliantly clear, so a night here is a good way to break a long ride.
t.nakuru@-0.3,36.1:
Nakuru lies on the floor of the Rift Valley at about 1,850 metres, a bustling farming and market city that serves a rich agricultural region. It has about 260,000 people, so everything is here: fuel, banks, hotels, workshops, supermarkets. The name comes from a Maasai word meaning place of dust, and in the dry season you can see why. Beside the town lies Lake Nakuru, a shallow soda lake that is protected as a national park, and it is famous for the flocks of flamingos that feed on the algae in the water, sometimes in hundreds of thousands, though numbers vary with the water level.

The park is one of the best in Kenya for seeing rhinos, both black and white, as well as Rothschild's giraffes, buffalo and lions, and leopards in the acacia woods. A fence encloses it, which makes it a safer and smaller place than the big savannah parks, and it is easy to visit in half a day. The lake level has risen strongly in recent years, flooding roads and changing the flamingo patterns, so conditions vary.

The road into Nakuru from Nairobi is a major highway, and the escarpment section is the finest part, with steep climbs, long descents and sweeping views of the volcanic landscape. Heavy trucks carrying goods to Uganda use it, and the road has a poor reputation for accidents, so overtake with great care and avoid riding at night. Surface quality changes: patches of excellent tarmac give way to potholes and broken edges. Weather is generally pleasant, although afternoon thunderstorms are common in the wet seasons.

For food, Nakuru is a place to try Kenyan staples: roast goat or beef, chapati, sukuma wiki, a dish of braised greens, and sweet milky chai. Markets sell fresh vegetables, and the district is known for its farms. The surrounding hills have extinct volcanoes, such as Menengai, with a huge crater that can be visited for a view over the whole valley. As a finish, the town is an easy place to rest, with plenty of places to sleep, and the wildlife of the lake is a few minutes away.
t.solnechnogorsk@56.2,37.0:
If you leave Moscow northwest on the old road to Saint Petersburg, Solnechnogorsk is roughly where the suburbs finally let go. It is a town of nearly sixty thousand, on the shore of Lake Senezh, with the usual jumble of Soviet blocks, new apartment towers, wooden houses and dachas, and it is a place most people drive straight through. The name means Sun Mountain Town, a Soviet invention of the late 1930s, though the settlement is older, and the lake is the only real attraction: a long, shallow stretch of water, popular with fishermen and weekend swimmers.

The reason to care about the road is history. The route between the two capitals is the one Peter the Great's successors used, the Tsar's road, along which carriages, armies and later Pushkin's heroes jolted for days, with posting stations every few dozen kilometres. The railway between them opened in 1851, and the highway followed the same corridor, so for centuries this has been the main artery of Russian power. Just beyond Solnechnogorsk, Klin holds the house where Tchaikovsky spent his last years, now a museum, a pleasant side trip if you have time.

On a motorcycle, the corridor is quick and dull. The old highway and the newer toll motorway run in parallel, with heavy lorry traffic, speed cameras and a high rate of overtaking by people in a hurry. The tolled route is smoother, and the older road passes through villages and has more bends, but also more hazards: crossings, parked cars, and potholes. Weekends are the worst, when Muscovites stream out to their country houses. Mornings are better, and weekday afternoons toward Moscow are crawling. In winter, the surface is salt and slush, and in summer, rain showers can make the tarmac greasy.

The town is a natural place to refuel. Petrol stations line the roads, supermarkets and cafés are plentiful, and it is a good point to check your bike and take a proper break after the first stretch. Accommodation is simple. Roadside cafés serve decent hot food, usually soup, dumplings and tea, and you can eat well for little.

Walk to the lake edge, if the day is bright. In the quiet beyond the traffic, the water is calm.
t.kolomenskoye@55.7,37.7:
Kolomenskoye is a royal village that the city grew around, and it still feels like a village, with apple orchards and open meadows on a high bank above the Moskva River. The Grand Princes of Moscow kept a country estate here from the fourteenth century, and Ivan the Terrible was born here in 1530. The star of the place is the Church of the Ascension, completed in 1532, a tall, white, tent-roofed church that rises from its base like a rocket, with no interior pillars and a design that has no earlier parallel in Russian stone architecture. It is on the UNESCO World Heritage List, and it is one of the most distinctive buildings in Moscow, partly because it feels so different from the onion domes of the Kremlin.

The surrounding park is large and green, with ancient oaks, rolling slopes, and the old wooden gates and towers moved here from other parts of the country. Peter the Great's small log cabin, brought from Arkhangelsk, stands on the grounds, and so does a reconstruction of a wooden palace of Tsar Alexei, a sprawling fantasy of carved gables that was destroyed in the eighteenth century. In autumn, the apple trees are loaded with fruit, and the smell is wonderful. Locals come here to walk, picnic and watch the river, and the views across the water toward the city are fine.

For a rider, Kolomenskoye is a destination within the city, not a place for a leisurely approach. Moscow's traffic is dense, and the main roads are wide, fast and crowded, with strict lane discipline and many cameras. The weekday rush hours are brutal, and weekends are better, especially mornings. Parking near the park can be tight, so plan ahead, and the side streets have some cobbles and tram tracks. Rain makes the road markings slick, and in winter, the city is under snow and salt.

Fuel is easy, since Moscow has stations everywhere, along with cafés, restaurants and hotels at every price. Within the park, there are small cafés and a market selling honey, and the gates close in the evening, so check the opening hours before you set out.

Walk up to the church, and look at it from the river side. The proportions make it seem to float.
t.novodevichy@55.7,37.6:
Novodevichy Convent sits in a bend of the Moskva River, and its walls and towers look like a pared-down version of the Kremlin, which is exactly the point. Grand Prince Vasily III founded it in 1524, to commemorate the capture of Smolensk from the Lithuanians, and it became one of the richest convents in the country, a place where women of noble families took the veil and where tsarevnas were confined. Peter the Great sent his half-sister Sophia here after she tried to seize power, and the memory lingers in the quiet courtyards. The ensemble of white walls, red-brick towers, golden domes, and a tall baroque bell tower is among the best preserved in Moscow, and was added to the UNESCO list in 2004.

Next to the convent is a cemetery that is almost a national pantheon. After the 1930s, it became a place where the country's cultural and political figures were buried, and the list is remarkable. The writers Chekhov, Gogol and Bulgakov rest here, along with the composers Prokofiev and Shostakovich, the film-maker Eisenstein, Nikita Khrushchev, with a famous black and white monument, and Boris Yeltsin. The stones range from plain slabs to sculpted portraits, and the leafy paths are quiet. A small fee is normally charged, and it is worth buying a map of the graves.

The area has the calm of a quiet corner of a huge city, with a pond where the swans of Tchaikovsky's ballet are said to have been inspired, beside the walls. A short distance away, the Luzhniki stadium and the Sparrow Hills viewpoint offer a look across the river toward the city centre. The Moscow University tower rises behind.

As a ride, this is a city one: heavy traffic, trams, multi-lane junctions, and strict lanes, with many speed cameras. The embankment roads are fast and straightforward, but the side streets can be tight, and parking close to the convent is limited. The best time is early morning on a weekend, when the streets are empty. In winter, snow and salt make the surface treacherous, and in summer, afternoon thunderstorms can drench you.

Fuel and food are plentiful, as in the rest of the capital, and there are cafés beside the park. Hours for the convent vary, and it is closed one day a week, so check before you go. Stand in the courtyard for a moment, and listen for the bells. They carry far across the river.
t.kaya jibana@-3.8,39.7:
A kaya is a sacred forest, and for the Mijikenda peoples of the Kenyan coast it was once much more: a fortified hilltop village hidden in the trees, a place of ancestral graves, ceremonies and council. Kaya Jibana, belonging to the Jibana community, sits in the hills inland from the coast between Mombasa and Kilifi, and it is one of a group of kaya forests listed by UNESCO in 2008. People no longer live inside, but elders still guard it, and entry is regulated by customs that visitors should respect: guides, permission, and no cutting or taking.

The forest is a remnant of the coastal woodland that once covered this region, a dense patch of tall trees, vines and shrubs that holds rare plants, butterflies and birds in a landscape otherwise given over to farms. Around it, the hills are covered in coconut palms, cashew trees and mango orchards, with small villages of mud-walled houses and roofs of thatch or tin. Nearby Rabai is where the first Christian mission in East Africa was established in the nineteenth century by the German missionary Johann Ludwig Krapf, and a small museum there tells the story.

The roads in are a mix of tarmac and red dirt, which turns to slick mud in the rainy seasons, roughly April to June and October to December. Main roads, especially the Mombasa–Nairobi highway, are dominated by trucks, buses and matatus, and the motorbike taxis called boda-bodas weave everywhere. Inland, quieter murram roads wind through the hills with views back to the ocean on clear days. Riding at night is best avoided, given poor lighting, livestock and unpredictable traffic.

Fuel is available in Mariakani on the highway, as well as in Mombasa and Kilifi, but small villages may only have petrol sold in bottles. Carry water, a hat and sun protection, as the coastal heat and humidity are intense. Local food includes coconut-based dishes, cassava and fresh fruit, and roadside stalls sell mandazi, sweet fried bread, with spiced tea. Arrange your visit through the local community or the museums' office to ensure a guide is available.
t.jebelal a la qalbloze@36.2,36.6:
High on the limestone ridge of the Jebel al-A'la, in the north west of Syria near the Turkish border, stands one of the most beautiful early Christian churches anywhere. The basilica of Qalb Lozeh was built in the second half of the fifth century, probably as a pilgrimage church on the route to the shrine of Saint Simeon Stylites, the hermit who spent decades living on top of a pillar not far to the east. Its facade, with a great arch flanked by two towers, is one of the earliest examples of a design that would later be repeated in the Romanesque churches of Europe. The church is part of the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, a UNESCO site listed in 2011, which includes some forty villages abandoned between the eighth and tenth centuries, often known as the Dead Cities.

These villages, scattered across the limestone hills between Aleppo and Idlib, were prosperous farming communities in late antiquity, growing olives, grapes and grain and exporting oil and wine across the Mediterranean. When trade routes shifted and the region's economy declined, they were gradually abandoned, and their stone houses, churches, olive presses and tombs were left standing, remarkably well preserved, in the dry hills.

The honest truth is that this region has been at the heart of Syria's long war, and for years it was off limits to visitors, with fighting, destruction and humanitarian crisis. The political situation in the country has changed since late 2024, but conditions remain uncertain, and many governments still advise strongly against travel. Anyone thinking of visiting should check the latest official advice and seek local knowledge. Several of the ancient sites have been damaged, and some are used as shelters by displaced families.

On a map, the area lies close to the Turkish border town of Reyhanlı, and the landscape on both sides is similar, with red soil, olive groves and grey limestone hills. If and when it becomes possible to ride here safely, the roads through the hills offer an unforgettable journey through a landscape of ancient ruins, with columns and arches standing among the olive trees. Until then, the photographs and the books will have to do, and the thought that this extraordinary place has survived so much is reason enough to hope.
t.jebel zawiye 2 rouweiha@35.7,36.7:
Scattered across the limestone hills of north-western Syria, between Aleppo and Idlib, lie hundreds of abandoned villages from late antiquity, built of finely cut stone between the first and seventh centuries and then gradually deserted. They are known as the Dead Cities, and together they form the World Heritage site of the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria. Ruweiha, in the Jebel Zawiye, is one of the largest: houses, churches, tombs and oil presses spread over a wide area, and among them the church of Bizzos, named after a local notable whose domed tomb stands beside it, is one of the best preserved. These villages grew rich on olive oil and trade, and their stone architecture, with arched doorways, carved lintels and crosses, is remarkably intact.

The landscape is stony and dry, with red soil between the limestone outcrops, olive groves and fields of wheat and vegetables. In spring the hills are green and dotted with wild flowers, in summer the heat bakes the stones. For centuries, shepherds and farmers lived among the ruins, and sometimes in them.

It has to be said plainly: this region has been at the centre of the Syrian war since 2011, and the Idlib province was one of the most heavily fought-over areas. Many ancient sites have been damaged, looted or used by armed groups. The political situation has changed significantly since the fall of the former government at the end of 2024, but security, landmines and unexploded ordnance remain real dangers, and conditions can change quickly. Anyone thinking of riding here must check current travel advice carefully, travel with reliable local contacts and accept that this is not, for now, an ordinary touring destination.

In calmer times, the roads between Saraqib, Kafranbel, Maarat al-Numan and the villages of the Jebel Zawiye were narrow and winding, crossing the hills through olive groves, with the main north-south highway nearby. Saraqib, about seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and shops. Syrian food, wherever you find it, is excellent: hummus, fresh bread, grilled meats, and the sweets of Aleppo, famous throughout the Middle East. The hospitality of ordinary people has survived everything.
t.sacred mijikenda kaya forests@-3.9,39.6:
Along the Kenyan coast, behind the resort hotels and the palm-lined beaches, there are scraps of forest that matter more to local people than almost any building. These are the kaya, the sacred forests of the Mijikenda, a group of nine related peoples including the Giriama and Digo, who say their ancestors settled in fortified villages hidden in the woods. Each kaya was a clearing in the trees, with a ring of defence and a set of elders who held the village's laws and ceremonies, and when the villages were abandoned, the forests were kept as places of prayer and burial.

Eleven of these forests were listed by UNESCO in 2008, and they hold some of the last remnants of the coastal forest that once ran all along East Africa, with rare plants, birds and butterflies. The paths are used by elders for ceremonies, and visiting means going with a local guide and permission, taking off hats, dressing modestly and following the rules.

The roads inland from Mombasa are hot, busy and humid. The A109 to Nairobi, a heavy-goods road with lorries, buses and boda-boda motorbikes, passes Mariakani, and on the older roads the surface can be patchy, with potholes and loose gravel. Sunrise is the best time, before traffic builds and the heat rises. Rains come in April to June and again around November, and when they come the red earth tracks turn into slick mud. Keep a good distance from lorries and expect sudden stops.

Mariakani is large enough to have fuel stations, small restaurants and shops, and Mombasa, a little over an hour away, has everything. In Mombasa, Fort Jesus, a Portuguese fortress built at the end of the sixteenth century, is worth seeing, and nearby Rabai has the site of the first Christian mission in East Africa, from the 1840s. Drink bottled water, carry sun protection, and take advice before leaving the main road.
t.jebel sem an 3 sinkhar@36.3,36.9:
The limestone massif north-west of Aleppo, in Syria, is one of the most remarkable archaeological landscapes in the Middle East, but it has also been in a war zone for more than a decade, and travel there is not safe or practical. What follows is about what the place is, not an invitation to visit.

From the fourth to the seventh centuries, the stony hills here carried dozens of prosperous villages, built in local limestone with an elegance that has survived better than almost anywhere else of that age. Houses, churches, bathhouses, tombs and olive presses stand in rows, many with two storeys, porches, carved lintels and decorative bands, and they are known today as the Dead Cities. Villagers prospered on olive oil, which was sold across the late Roman world, and when the trade shifted and conquest came, the villages gradually emptied, leaving their stone buildings to the weather. In 2011 UNESCO listed a group of these as the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria.

The most famous site is the church of Saint Simeon, near here, built in the fifth century around the pillar on which Simeon the Stylite lived for decades, preaching to crowds of pilgrims who came to see him. The huge cruciform basilica, with four wings radiating from an octagon, was one of the largest churches of its time and still has fine carved arches, though it has been damaged in recent fighting. Nubl, the nearest sizeable town, is also in a conflict-affected area.

Anyone interested should follow the work of archaeologists and conservation groups, who have documented the condition of the sites, and look at photographs and survey drawings rather than plan a trip. Government travel advice for the area is clear, and fuel supplies, roads and security are all unreliable. If conditions change in the future, this will be one of the great journeys of the region, among olive groves and honey-coloured stone, but that day has not come yet.
t.kaya giriama@-3.8,39.5:
Behind the beaches of Kenya's north coast, on the low red ridges inland from Kilifi, sit a string of forest patches that look like nothing much from the road. They are the kayas, once the fortified villages of the Mijikenda peoples, the nine related groups that include the Giriama, and today they are the sacred groves where elders still gather. The Kaya Giriama forest is one of them, and part of a UNESCO listing that covers several of these remnants of coastal forest. The village huts were long ago abandoned and the clearings overgrown, but the grove survives because it is protected by custom, so that cutting a tree or entering without permission is a serious matter.

What you find here, then, is more of a woodland than a monument. It is a fragment of the East African coastal forest, rich in species found nowhere else, with huge old trees, shade that drops the temperature by several degrees, birds, butterflies, and probably a few rustling things in the leaf litter. The elders keep the sacred sites, hold meetings and rituals, and receive visitors with a mixture of courtesy and caution, so arrange a visit through the local committee or a guide rather than wandering in. Ask before taking pictures, and expect to leave a small donation.

The roads here are a pleasant jumble. The main highway from Mombasa to Nairobi passes through Mariakani, about eight kilometres from this point, and from there the smaller roads wander through cashew trees, coconut palms, mango orchards and maize patches, with red dust in the dry months and mud in the long rains from April to June. The tarmac gives out and the murram begins faster than the map suggests, and potholes, goats, bicycles and boda-boda motorcycles share the track. Watch the heat and carry water, because the humidity builds fast.

Mariakani is a busy highway town with fuel, roadside food and plenty of trucks, and it is the sensible place to prepare, since the villages around the kaya are small and may have no pump. Kilifi and Mombasa, both within a couple of hours, have all the services you would want, and the sea is within reach when you need a swim. Roadside stalls sell roasted cashews and sugarcane. Mornings are best, with softer light under the canopy, and sunset comes quickly, so aim to be back on the tarmac by dusk.
t.rostov veliky@57.2,39.4:
Rostov, known as Rostov Veliky, or Rostov the Great, is one of the oldest towns in Russia, mentioned in the earliest chronicles under the year 862, and it sits on the shore of Lake Nero, a broad, shallow lake in the Yaroslavl region. Its history gives it a quiet grandeur that few other provincial towns can match. The Kremlin, built in the seventeenth century as the residence of the metropolitan, stands beside the water, a long, white walled enclosure of churches, towers and gardens, and its bells, cast in the 1680s, still ring out across the lake in a famous peal.

The town is part of the Golden Ring of old cities northeast of Moscow, and travellers have been coming here for centuries. It has a long tradition of enamel painting, known as finift, in which tiny, brightly coloured scenes are painted on metal, and workshops still make brooches, boxes and icons. Local gardeners are known for their onions, grown in the rich soil of the lake shore and sold in markets around the region, and the town's cuisine has a modest, hearty character that suits cold weather.

The roads in this region are flat, wide and straight, with little change in gradient. The main highway between Moscow and Yaroslavl runs close by, busy with trucks, and quieter local roads wander through villages of wooden houses with carved window frames, birch woods and fields. Surface quality varies, with smooth new asphalt in some places and potholes and patches in others, so keep your eyes on the road. Summer is the best season, with long evenings and warm weather, while spring brings mud and winter brings snow and ice.

Rostov has about thirty thousand people and enough fuel stations, shops and cafés to meet your needs, and Ishnya, a few kilometres away, is a smaller place with a few shops. The nearest big city is Yaroslavl, about sixty kilometres to the north, which has a fine riverside and a number of old churches covered in painted tiles. If you plan to ride the Golden Ring, allow time to wander the streets and see the churches, because the real pleasure of the region is not in the kilometres but in the stops. Pereslavl, on its own lake to the south, is a worthy partner for a day's ride.
t.kolomna@55.1,38.8:
Kolomna stands where the Moskva River flows into the Oka, about a hundred kilometres southeast of Moscow, and the confluence has made it a town of consequence for more than eight centuries. Its Kremlin, built in the early 1500s on the orders of Grand Prince Vasily III to guard the southern approaches to Moscow, still has long stretches of brick wall and several towers, and it is one of the most evocative old fortifications in the region. One of the towers served as a prison in the early seventeenth century, and it is said that Marina Mniszech, the Polish wife of the false Dmitry, died there in 1614.

The town has also been an industrial centre for a long time. The Kolomna works, founded in the 1860s, built locomotives and heavy engines that went all across Russia, and the factory remains a landmark. But Kolomna's greatest claim to local pride is the pastila, a delicate, tart sweet made from apples and egg white, which has been produced here for generations and is served in a museum devoted to it, where visitors can taste several kinds with tea. It makes an excellent, light snack for a rider with a long day ahead.

The ride follows the Oka westward and then south, towards Ryazan, through a landscape of broad meadows, birch groves and low bluffs above the river. The roads are straight and flat, the corners are rare and the traffic can be heavy near Moscow and light farther south. Surface quality varies, so keep your eyes open for potholes, and be aware that wooden bridges and level crossings are still found on some secondary roads. Summer evenings are long and warm, and the smell of hay and wood smoke drifts across the fields. In winter the roads can be icy and the days are short.

With nearly a hundred and fifty thousand people, Kolomna has plenty of fuel, food and accommodation, so it is a good place to fill up before a long day. Sychyovo and Raduzhny, small settlements nearby, have a few shops and cafés, but not much more. If you want to see the town properly, give yourself a couple of hours to walk the Kremlin walls, visit the pastila museum and look down over the water from the old embankment, where fishermen sit in all weathers.
t.ngorongoro crater rim@-3.2,35.6:
On the rim of Ngorongoro the first thing that hits you is the cold. At around 2,300 metres the air is thin and damp, the forest is wrapped in mist most mornings, and the wind whips over the edge of the caldera with a bite that surprises people who think of Africa as hot. Then the mist tears and the floor appears about six hundred metres below, a vast grassy bowl twenty kilometres across, with a lake glinting in the middle and tiny dots of animals scattered over the plain. It is one of the great views on the planet, and it takes a while to understand the scale.

The crater is the remains of a giant volcano that collapsed in on itself two or three million years ago. It is the largest intact caldera in the world, and the walls act like a fence, holding a dense population of wildlife: wildebeest, zebra, buffalo, lions, hyenas, flamingos on the soda lake and some of the last black rhinos in Tanzania. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and part of a conservation area where Maasai herders live alongside the animals, grazing their cattle on the highlands. You will see them walking the road in red robes, carrying sticks, with great dignity.

The road along the rim, from Karatu to Lodoare gate, is a good, smooth climb through cloud forest, with big trees draped in lichen, tight bends and fog. Beyond, the route to Olduvai Gorge and the Serengeti is rougher and drier, with stretches of dust and corrugation. Rules for motorcycles in the conservation area are strict, and entry fees are high, so you must check access, permits and guide requirements in advance. Wildlife can be on the road, and elephants and buffalo have right of way.

Fuel is available at Karatu, a pleasant highland town of about twenty thousand people to the east, and it is wise to be full before climbing, as there is nothing reliable on the rim. Lodges along the edge serve meals and rooms at a price, but a picnic at a viewpoint is fine too.

Olduvai Gorge, further on, is where Mary and Louis Leakey found some of the oldest remains of early humans, and the small museum is worth a visit. Look for the Maasai villages as you ride, and respect their privacy.
t.myshkin@57.8,38.5:
Myshkin is a small town on the Volga, about two hundred kilometres north of Moscow, and it is one of those places that has made a virtue of its smallness. About six thousand people live here in a cluster of old merchant houses, churches and wooden cottages on the river bank, at a point where the great river, broad and brown, rolls slowly past. The town grew rich from river trade in the nineteenth century and still has a tidy, provincial look, with a long street of two-storey brick houses and a cathedral with a tall bell tower.

The name is said to come from the Russian word for mouse, and the town has embraced the idea with enthusiasm. A local legend tells how a mouse saved the town's founder, a prince, from a snake, and the mouse is now the town's symbol. A museum devoted entirely to mice displays thousands of mouse figures, toys, and paintings, and is surprisingly entertaining, with an interactive exhibition that has delighted children and adults for decades. There are other small museums too, some of them gloriously quirky, and a number of craft shops sell souvenirs.

The surroundings are more serious. The Volga here is part of a chain of huge reservoirs built in the Soviet era, and the Rybinsk Reservoir, a short distance north, was flooded in the early 1940s, drowning the old town of Mologa and many villages. On the other side of the river, Uglich, with its brightly painted churches and the famous Church of St Dmitry on the Blood, is within easy reach. The riverbanks are lined with willow and birch, and in summer the water is busy with pleasure boats and cruise ships.

Riding to Myshkin is a gentle journey on flat roads through farmland and forest, and the surface is mostly good, though patched in places. Fuel is best found in Uglich or Rybinsk, the nearest towns with larger populations, since Myshkin itself is small, and the distances between services can be long. Summer is warm and the evenings are light until late, while winter is long, dark and cold, with snow and ice. A walk along the embankment at sunset, watching the river turn pink and the boats slide past, is the best way to end a day here.
t.new jerusalem monastery@55.9,36.8:
The monastery at Istra is a replica of Jerusalem, and the man who built it never meant it as a joke. Patriarch Nikon, the most powerful churchman in seventeenth-century Russia, founded New Jerusalem in 1656, and he set out to recreate the holy places of Palestine in the Russian countryside. The great Resurrection Cathedral copies the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, with a vast rotunda over a representation of the tomb, and the river nearby was renamed the Jordan, the hills around it given the names of Tabor and Olivet. For a while it was one of the most ambitious building projects in the country.

Nikon fell out with Tsar Alexei, and was stripped of his office and exiled, and the monastery was left unfinished for years. The architecture that followed is lovely in a restless way, with towers, tiled stoves and decorated walls. In December 1941, during the battle for Moscow, retreating German troops blew up the cathedral and the bell tower, leaving a smoking ruin. The restoration took decades, and the rebuilt rotunda is a quiet testimony to the effort. Inside, the cathedral is a vast, echoing space, and from the walls you can see the winding river and the fields beyond.

For a rider coming out of Moscow this is a natural half-day, close to the capital but far enough to feel like a different world. The roads in the area run west of the city through woodland, small towns and old villages, and the surface, as in most of the Moscow region, can be uneven, with patched asphalt and the odd hole, so it pays to keep an eye on the road ahead. Weekend traffic is heavy, and the main roads through Istra can be slow, so set off early. In the morning, the walls are quiet and the light on the stone is lovely.

Istra is a town of over thirty thousand people and has everything you need: fuel, cafes, shops and a few places to sit with a view of the walls. It makes sense to eat here rather than looking for something near the monastery, where the options are limited and expensive. Check opening times for the cathedral before you come, since the monastery is a museum and has its own schedule, and carry something to cover your head and shoulders if you plan to enter the church.
t.borodino@55.5,35.8:
Borodino is a field, and what happened here on the seventh of September 1812 is hard to grasp until you stand on it. Napoleon's army, marching on Moscow, met the Russian army under Kutuzov on this rolling plain west of the capital, and in a single day the two sides lost something like seventy thousand men killed and wounded, one of the bloodiest days of the Napoleonic wars. Neither could claim to have won outright. The Russians withdrew, the French took Moscow a week later, and the war went on to its famous conclusion in the winter snow.

The battlefield has been kept open and largely unbuilt, which is its greatest strength. The land is a gentle patchwork of fields and copses, with the ground rising here and there to the places where the fighting was fiercest: the Raevsky Redoubt, where the Russian guns held the centre, and the flèches, the arrowhead-shaped earthworks that Bagration defended. Monuments in granite and bronze stand on the ridges, many of them raised in 1912 for the centenary, and others added by regiments and families. The Spaso-Borodino Monastery, founded by the widow of one of the fallen generals, stands quietly at one edge. Tolstoy visited the field while writing War and Peace, and the book gives it a place in the imagination that no museum can match.

The riding to Borodino is mostly straightforward. The roads cross open farmland and low forest, with long straights and gentle bends, and on a fine day it is easy riding with a lot of sky. The main routes from Moscow carry heavy freight and a lot of weekend traffic, so use the minor roads where you can, and be wary of potholes, which can be deep after winter. In early September, the battle is re-enacted by hundreds of costumed volunteers in a spectacle that draws huge crowds, and the roads around the field are closed or crowded, so choose your day with care.

Mozhaysk, thirteen kilometres away, is the town for fuel and a meal, with a population of over thirty thousand and a good old centre that includes a kremlin and a cathedral. At the field itself the services are limited to a small museum and a cafe or two. Bring something to drink and be ready to walk, because the monuments are spread over a wide area, and a bike will only take you to some of them. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the light is low and the fields are quiet.
t.yakhroma@56.3,37.5:
Yakhroma sits on a canal, and the canal is what matters. The Moscow Canal, which links the capital to the Volga, was dug in the 1930s by tens of thousands of workers, many of them prisoners, and when it opened in 1937 it brought the river to the city and gave Moscow the water supply and the port it had lacked. The canal passes through Yakhroma, and the locks and the pumping stations that serve it were built in a grand style, with towers and ornamental gates, so that even the industrial architecture has a ceremonial feel.

The little river that gave the town its name runs through the old centre, and the town grew up around textile mills that processed cotton and linen. Today it is a modest place of about twelve thousand people, with a mix of Soviet apartment blocks, old brick factory buildings and wooden houses with carved window frames. The waterfront by the lock is a pleasant place to sit and watch the barges. In summer, people come here to swim and fish, and anglers sit along the banks of the canal at all hours.

Nearby Dmitrov, seven kilometres away, is much older, and has a better story. It was founded in 1154 by Yuri Dolgoruky, the prince credited with founding Moscow, and the earthen ramparts of its kremlin still encircle the cathedral at the centre of town. The anarchist thinker Peter Kropotkin spent his last years here, and died in the town in 1921. The roads between the two towns run through flat, farmed country with birch woods and wide fields, and the road is usually well kept along the main route, with narrower lanes in the villages.

For a rider, this is gentle country, a place for a relaxed ride rather than an exciting one. The road along the canal has a quiet charm, with long, straight stretches broken by bridges and locks, and in the early morning, the mist rising off the water is lovely. Traffic is heavier on the approaches to Dmitrov and on weekends, when Muscovites head for their dachas. Fuel is available in Yakhroma itself and in Dmitrov, which has everything else you could need, including a good choice of cafes. Autumn and early spring are the best times, when the birches are bare or turning and the canal is calm.
t.zavidovo@56.5,36.5:
Zavidovo is known across Russia less for the village than for the forest that surrounds it. That huge woodland, between the Volga and the Shosha rivers, was set aside in the 1930s as a hunting reserve for the Soviet leadership, and generations of officials hunted its elk, deer and wild boar behind fences and checkpoints. Today the core of the reserve is a national park, and the woods that surround it are among the richest in the Moscow region, with spruce, pine and birch stands, marshes and quiet lakes.

The Volga is the other force in the landscape. Here the river was dammed in the 1930s to create the Ivankovo Reservoir, known as the Moscow Sea, a large artificial lake that feeds the Moscow Canal and gives the capital its drinking water. The shore at Zavidovo is a favourite spot for anglers, sailors and weekenders from the capital, and the village has grown to a sizeable settlement of several thousand, with a mix of old wooden houses, new summer homes and the sort of leisure facilities that the reservoir brings.

The old M10 highway runs through here, and it is one of the busiest roads in Russia, carrying a huge amount of freight between Moscow and St Petersburg. Riding it is a matter of patience, with trucks, roadworks and average speed controls. The better experience is on the quiet roads that run through the forest and along the shore of the reservoir, where the surface is variable but the traffic is slight. The woods are most beautiful in autumn, when birch and aspen turn yellow among the dark conifers, and the mushroom pickers come out in force, so watch for cars parked along the verges.

Zavidovo has fuel, shops and a few cafes, with a population of seven thousand or so, and Novozavidovsky, a short way off, is similar. It is a practical place to stop on the way between Moscow and Tver, and there is enough food and rest to make it worthwhile. If you are interested in nature, check whether the park allows access on the day, since parts of the reserve are restricted. Summer evenings by the water are pleasant, but the mosquitoes are numerous in the woods, so carry repellent.
t.hogpen gap@34.7,-83.9:
Hogpen Gap is the sort of name that sounds like a joke until you ride up to it. It is a notch in the crest of the Blue Ridge in the Chattahoochee National Forest, in north Georgia, where the Richard B. Russell Scenic Highway, State Route 348, crests the ridge and drops down the far side. The road is named for a long-serving senator from the state, and it is one of the few in Georgia that feels like a real mountain pass, with a good deal of rock, dark rhododendron thickets and the smell of damp hardwood leaves.

From the Helen side it is a proper climb. The highway goes up through tight, quick bends, some of them hairpins, with steep wooded drops on the outside and the odd gravel patch where rain has washed the verge. Cut-in pull-offs let you look across ridge after ridge in the blue haze that gives the range its name; on a still October morning the view is exactly the one on the postcards. Brasstown Bald, the highest point in Georgia, is a short way off, and the Appalachian Trail wanders along the ridges nearby, so there are often walkers at the pull-offs.

It helps to know that this is also where the gold fever of the 1820s began. Dahlonega, down the hill to the south-west, saw the first major gold rush in the United States, in 1828, before California was anyone's idea. The Cherokee, whose land this was, were pushed out in the following decade on the Trail of Tears, and the name of the nearby town comes from a Cherokee word for yellow. The Cherokee name for the whole area lingers on in rivers and gaps.

Nothing is sold at the gap itself, and the nearest towns are small, so plan your tank before you start. Dahlonega is the nearest place of any size, twenty-seven kilometres off, with a square full of cafes, shops and the old courthouse that is now a gold museum; Cleveland and Blairsville are the other places to try. Autumn weekends bring a procession of cars, bikes and tour buses, so go on a weekday if you can, and aim for the early morning, when the cold air lies in the hollows and the sun hits the ridges first. Frost can linger on shaded bends well into spring.
t.turners corner@34.6,-83.8:
Turners Corner is a crossroads, and in this corner of Georgia that is enough to make it a landmark. Where several of the old mountain roads meet in the foothills of the Blue Ridge, a small store and a gravel lay-by have served as a meeting point for riders for a long time, and on a Saturday morning there are always a few bikes parked in the lot, with their riders arguing amiably about which loop to take. It is not a place to spend an afternoon, but it is a good place to be at nine o'clock.

The country around it is a mix of pastureland, small orchards and wooded ridges, with creek valleys running between them. Roads here were laid out by farmers and loggers, not engineers, and they follow the contours, which means that every kilometre has a bend in it. North of the corner the land rises toward the high gaps, and the roads over them are the real prizes; to the south, the rolling hills run down toward Dahlonega and the gold country. Cleveland is the nearest town, seven kilometres away, and it has an odd claim to fame: it is the home of the doll hospital where Cabbage Patch Kids are, in the story at least, born.

Dahlonega's mint once stamped gold coins from the local ore, and the story of the place is a story of fortune and its aftermath. When the gold ran thin, the people turned to apples, timber and, later, tourism. Apple season in September and October brings cider, fried pies and stalls along the road, and if you are lucky you will find a farm stand selling jam. Some of the better roads are narrow, with blind bends and no shoulder, so keep your speed measured, particularly on weekends when the area is full of visitors.

Fuel is no trouble at either end: Cleveland has stations on the main road, and Dahlonega, seventeen kilometres away, has several more. The corner itself offers a cold drink and a snack, and little else. Spring brings the dogwoods and redbuds, and summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms building over the ridges in the afternoon. The best light, as ever in the mountains, comes in the hour after dawn and the hour before dusk, and the roads are quietest then.
t.suches@34.7,-84.0:
Locals call Suches the valley above the clouds, which is both accurate and a good piece of marketing. It is a small high basin in the Blue Ridge, ringed by mountains and cool in summer, with a hamlet at its centre, a school, a few shops and not much else. It sits at an elevation that makes it one of the few places in Georgia where snow regularly lies, and in winter the surrounding roads can be icy long after the lowlands have thawed.

What makes it famous among riders is the road. State Route 60 climbs out of the valley over Woody Gap, one of the high saddles of the Blue Ridge, where the Appalachian Trail crosses the road and walkers gather at the overlook, and then descends toward Dahlonega through forest in a long run of dips, curves and short straights. Another favourite, Wolf Pen Gap Road, wriggles up and over a neighbouring ridge with a succession of hairpins and tight, narrow bends that demand concentration; it is narrow, with a poor surface in places, and sees plenty of gravel and fallen leaves. Cyclists share these roads, and in good weather you may find yourself among a small crowd.

The history of the area is the history of the Cherokee and of the gold seekers who displaced them. Lake Winfield Scott, a small reservoir in the forest nearby, offers camping and a swim, and Blood Mountain, one of the highest points on the Appalachian Trail in Georgia, rises to the north-east. The name Blood Mountain is said to come from a battle between the Cherokee and the Creek, though the story is hard to confirm. The forest here is hardwood, with oak, hickory and poplar, and in spring, wildflowers, flame azalea and mountain laurel.

Services in Suches are limited. There is no reliable fuel in the valley, so fill up in Dahlonega, twenty-one kilometres away, or Blairsville, and carry what you need for the day. A small store serves coffee and snacks, but most of the real food is in the larger towns. In autumn the colour is spectacular and the roads are crowded, so aim for a weekday; in winter, check whether the passes are icy before you set out. Mist often fills the valley in the morning, and the sun burns it off by ten.
t.hiawassee@34.9,-83.8:
Hiawassee is a lakeside town, and the lake is the thing. Lake Chatuge, a long, winding reservoir built by the Tennessee Valley Authority in the early 1940s, fills the valley, stretching across the state line into North Carolina, and its shoreline is a tangle of coves, wooded points and small marinas. The town of Hiawassee, with about nine hundred inhabitants, sits at the western end of it, a handful of streets of shops, cafes and motels along the main road, and the water is only a few minutes away.

The name comes from a Cherokee word usually given as Ayuhwasi, meaning a meadow, and this was Cherokee country long before the dam. The river that was drowned by the reservoir was one of the old arteries of the nation, and the valley was densely settled. The mountains that surround the lake, among them Brasstown Bald, the highest in Georgia, give the district a cool climate and good rainfall, and the forest on their slopes is thick with hemlock, oak and rhododendron. Each August the town hosts the Georgia Mountain Fair, which has been going for decades and has a festival feel, with music, crafts, and a lot of fried food.

Riding here is easy and enjoyable. US 76 runs along the lake, a wide, well-surfaced road with gentle bends and glimpses of the water, and from it you can turn into the hills on a variety of smaller roads. They have steeper gradients and tighter corners, with farms and the occasional church at the junctions. The lake road is much busier in summer, with boat trailers and holiday traffic, so take your time, and aim for the shoulder seasons if you can. Fog sits on the water in the morning, and in autumn the colour of the hills reflected in the lake is among the best in the Georgia mountains.

Hiawassee has fuel, groceries and a handful of restaurants, serving the usual Southern staples of fried chicken, barbecue and biscuits, so it is a good place to prepare for the hills. Young Harris, a few kilometres east, is home to a small college and has a pleasant old centre, and Hayesville, across the line in North Carolina, is a similar size. Cold nights are common even in late spring, so carry a warm layer.
t.unicoi gap@34.8,-83.7:
A gap is a low point on a ridge, and Unicoi Gap is one of the notable ones on the Georgia Blue Ridge. It carries State Route 75 over the crest between Helen and Hiawassee, and it is also where the Appalachian Trail crosses the road, so a pull-off and a trailhead sit at the top, and during the hiking season you will see boots, backpacks and sunburnt faces. The name is thought to come from a Cherokee word for white, or perhaps for fog, and the fog is certainly present on many mornings, rolling up out of the valleys and pooling at the gap.

The route over it is old. Before it was a modern highway, it was part of the Unicoi Turnpike, a Cherokee trading path that linked the settlements of the Georgia and Carolina valleys with those across the mountains in Tennessee, and in the early nineteenth century it was improved as a road for wagons and drovers. Traders, armies, missionaries and, in the late 1830s, the Cherokee marched on the Trail of Tears all passed through country like this. There is something sobering about riding a road that has carried so much history, and at the gap there is a wide view over the forested ridges that should give you a moment of quiet.

The riding is good. On the Helen side, the road climbs steadily out of the Chattahoochee valley through hardwood forest, with bends tightening toward the top and a surface that is mostly clean and well kept. On the other side, it drops through more forest before opening out into the farmland around Hiawassee. At the gap itself, the air is noticeably cooler than in the valleys, and a clear, windy day can feel several degrees colder than the thermometer in town. Autumn colour here peaks in mid-October, and the road is crowded then.

There are no services at the gap, so arrive with what you need. Helen, a Bavarian-style village with a lot of tourist attractions, is the nearest place with fuel on one side, and Hiawassee, about eighteen kilometres on the other, serves as the base for the lake. Early morning in October, with fog filling the valleys below and the ridge tops catching the first sun, is as good as the southern mountains get.
t.the rabai kayas@-3.9,39.6:
Behind Mombasa, a short ride inland, the coastal plain lifts into the red Rabai hills, and in the forest on their slopes sit the kayas. These are the sacred forest groves of the Mijikenda people, nine related peoples who say their ancestors came from a legendary homeland called Shungwaya. Each kaya was a fortified village in the forest, with a council of elders, and the groves are still looked after for ritual and burial. Several kayas are protected as a World Heritage site, and the Rabai group is one of the best known.

The ride from Mombasa takes you off the coast highway and onto smaller roads that wind past palms, cashew trees, mango groves and little roadside stalls with pineapples piled in pyramids. The red earth is the colour of brick, and the air is warm, humid and green, full of birdsong. Surface quality varies, so look out for potholes, speed bumps in every village and the matatus, the minibuses, that dominate the main road and overtake without warning. Pick a morning in the drier months, June to October or January to February, because the long rains of April and May turn side tracks to slippery red clay.

Rabai also has a place in the story of Kenya as a whole. It is where the first Christian mission station in East Africa was established, in the 1840s, by the German missionary Johann Ludwig Krapf, and the old church there is still known. The kayas themselves have a more ancient story. Visitors are generally accompanied by a local guide or elder, who explains the customs: what to wear, what not to touch, and where you may not go. Inside, the forest is dense and cool, with big old trees and the sense of a place that has been listened to for centuries. Colobus monkeys and many butterflies and birds live in these remnants of coastal forest, which once covered much of the coastline.

As for practical things, Mariakani, a bustling town of about thirteen thousand, and Mombasa itself have fuel, food and mechanics. Do not expect fuel in the villages. Take small cash for guides and contributions, dress modestly, and ask before photographing.
t.kirillov@59.9,38.4:
Kirillov is a quiet town of about seven thousand people in the Vologda region, and its whole reason for existing is the monastery that rises beside the lake. The Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery, founded in 1397 by a monk named Kirill, grew over the following centuries into one of the largest and richest in Russia, with massive walls and a ring of towers enclosing a whole collection of churches, bell towers and cells on the shore of Lake Siverskoye. In the medieval period, it was a fortress as well as a place of prayer, and tsars including Ivan the Terrible visited and sent people there in disgrace.

Inside the walls, the monastery has the atmosphere of a small walled city, with the white stone of the Assumption Cathedral shining against the dark water and sky. Today it is mainly a museum, with a famous collection of icons and old manuscripts, and some monastic life has returned. Walking along the ramparts gives a view over the lake and the gentle, wooded countryside, where mist often rises in the early morning. It is a quiet place, with few crowds outside the main summer season.

The surrounding land is flat and wet, with forest, bog, small rivers and big lakes, part of the region the Russians call the Russian North. The road from Vologda passes through villages with wooden houses, carved window frames and painted shutters, some of them in poor repair and some well kept. Ferapontovo, about twenty kilometres away, has another monastery with frescoes painted by the master Dionisy in 1502, a UNESCO site and among the finest surviving works of medieval Russian art. The colours, soft blues, ochres and greens, are still clear.

The riding is easy and unhurried, on narrow roads with moderate traffic, long straights and gentle bends. The surface can be rough, especially away from the main route, with patches and potholes that appear suddenly, and spring thaw makes it worse. Distances are long and the countryside is empty, so allow plenty of time. Summer evenings are very long, with a pale light that lasts until late, while in winter the roads are covered in snow and ice.

Kirillov has a few fuel stations and shops, and small cafes serving soup, pancakes and fish from the lakes. Goritsy and Kuzino, nearby villages, have fewer services, so top up in town before exploring. The monastery grounds have a small entrance fee, and the best light for photographs is in the late afternoon.
t.sergiev posad@56.3,38.1:
Sergiev Posad is the spiritual heart of Russian Orthodoxy, and the Trinity Lavra of St Sergius, its great monastery, is the reason. It was founded in the fourteenth century by Sergius of Radonezh, a hermit who became the most revered saint in Russia, and it grew into a fortified complex with white walls, blue and gold domes and towers painted in bright colours. It withstood a long siege by Polish forces in the early seventeenth century, and its fame as a centre of pilgrimage has never faded. Today it is again an active monastery and a UNESCO site, with crowds of pilgrims at weekends and on feast days.

The Lavra's central church, the Trinity Cathedral, holds the relics of St Sergius and an icon of the Trinity by Andrei Rublev, though the original is now in a Moscow gallery and a copy is on view. The Assumption Cathedral, built under Ivan the Terrible, has a blue ceiling spangled with gold stars. In the grounds, there are a spring said to have healing water and a large bell tower. Women are expected to cover their heads in the churches, and photography is limited in some places.

The town is also known for toys. Sergiev Posad was one of the centres of Russian wooden toy making, and the first matryoshka dolls were reportedly made in the region in the 1890s. A toy museum in town has historic examples, and shops along the main street sell painted wooden dolls, spoons and ornaments. The town has more than a hundred thousand people, with a busy centre and a lot of Soviet housing around it.

The road from Moscow, around seventy kilometres, is a major highway, busy with commuter traffic and trucks, so leave early on weekends. Beyond the town, the roads toward Pereslavl and Alexandrov are quieter and pass through fields, woods and old villages, with wooden houses and small churches. The surface varies, with patches of rough asphalt, and the best weather is in late spring and early autumn. In winter, the snow and frost make the domes look even more striking, though roads can be icy.

Fuel and food are easy in the town, with stations on the main road and cafes near the monastery, serving pies, soups and tea. Semkhoz and Skoropuskovsky are smaller places nearby. Take a scarf for your head and a bit of patience for the queues.
t.architectural ensemble of the trinity se:
Sergiyev Posad is where Russians go to pray and to buy a wooden toy, often on the same afternoon. About seventy kilometres north-east of Moscow, the town grew around the Trinity Lavra of Saint Sergius, a monastery founded in the fourteenth century by Sergius of Radonezh, a hermit who became the spiritual father of the nation. When Prince Dmitry Donskoy sought a blessing before facing the Tatars at Kulikovo in 1380, he is said to have come here, and ever since the monastery has been the most revered in the country, with pilgrims queuing in all weathers to touch the saint's relics.

Inside the white walls the buildings crowd together in a way that feels almost theatrical. The Dormition Cathedral, with its four blue domes spangled with gold stars, was modelled on the one in the Kremlin and commissioned by Ivan the Terrible, and the slim blue-and-white bell tower is a late baroque confection that rises over everything. Candles, incense and the sound of choirs fill the cathedrals, and old women in headscarves cross themselves with each step. Everything is alive, a working monastery with a seminary and a theological academy, and not a museum.

The town has another trade. For centuries craftsmen here carved wooden toys, and Sergiyev Posad is one of the places that claims the nesting doll, the matryoshka, as its own invention, and there is a toy museum a short walk from the walls. Local shops sell painted dolls, small carved animals and honey cakes, and a bag of such things is the standard souvenir.

The ride up from Moscow follows the old Yaroslavl road, one of the busiest corridors out of the capital, with heavy trucks, queues on Friday and Sunday and speed cameras at frequent intervals, so it is better to start early and go on a weekday. Beyond the town the roads become quieter, running through birch woods, small villages with carved window frames and wide fields, though the surface is often patched and rutted where the lorries have worn it down. Mosquitoes and midges in summer are real, and the autumn colours of birch and aspen are lovely.

Sergiyev Posad has more than a hundred thousand people, so fuel and food are simple, with stations on the main road and cafes around the monastery. Check the current rules on travel and documents for foreign visitors and vehicles before planning anything here, as they change often.
t.karlik site@38.6,35.0:
The Karlık church, one of the rock-cut sanctuaries of the district, is usually described as a dark church, with a simple cross-in-square plan cut into the stone and painted decoration that has faded over the centuries. Many rock churches here were cut by monks in the tenth and eleventh centuries, and their interiors imitate built architecture, with carved domes, pillars and arches that look like masonry but are all hollowed from a single mass of rock.

The point of visiting such a place is the quiet. There may be no ticket office, no bus park, and only a shepherd and his dog to share the view. The rock walls are pitted with pigeon holes, a reminder that for centuries villagers collected pigeon droppings to fertilise the vineyards and orchards, and painted the little dovecote entrances with white patterns. Hawks wheel above the ridge, and in spring the fields have poppies and wild mustard. In summer the heat from the rock is intense, and by late afternoon the stone turns a deep orange.

The riding on this side is easy and pleasant. Smooth country roads link the villages through vineyards and apricot orchards, with long views toward the snow-capped cone of Erciyes on a clear day. The traffic is light, and the hazards are tractors, flocks of sheep and the occasional unmarked speed bump at a village entrance. Autumn is lovely, with the harvest and golden leaves, and winter brings snow that closes minor tracks and turns the stone churches to white shells. Many of the rock churches in remote spots are locked or require a local guide, so ask in the nearest village.

Ürgüp, about ten kilometres away, has fuel, shops, good restaurants and several wine cellars, and it is a better base than the busier Göreme if you prefer calm. Take water with you, and wear boots with grip on the rock, which can be slippery with fine dust.
t.arslantepe mound@38.4,38.4:
Arslantepe is a tall mound on the plain just outside Malatya in eastern Turkey, and it hides one of the longest continuous stories of human settlement in the region. The name means lion hill, after the stone lions found at its gate, but the earliest layers go back to around 6000 BC, and the people who lived here over the next seven thousand years built, burned and rebuilt a succession of towns on the same spot. In the fourth millennium BC the site held a palace complex with storerooms, administrative rooms and wall paintings, which archaeologists regard as one of the earliest signs of organised state power in the Near East, with clay seals used to control the goods. Arslantepe also yielded some of the oldest known swords, made of arsenic bronze.

In the Iron Age the city became a capital of a small Neo-Hittite kingdom, called Melid, and a monumental gateway guarded by carved stone lions led into the citadel. The Assyrians took it in the eighth century BC. A pair of the stone lions is now in the Museum of Anatolian Civilisations in Ankara, though copies and parts of the gate remain on site. The mound was added to the World Heritage list in 2021, and visitors can walk among the mud-brick walls under a protective roof.

The setting is the broad valley of the Euphrates, with Malatya, the city of apricots, nearby, and the area is one of the biggest producers of dried apricots in the world. In early spring the orchards bloom white and pink across the plain. Malatya was badly damaged by the earthquake of February 2023, which hit eastern Turkey hard, and the city is still rebuilding, so visitors should expect road works and some closed buildings.

The riding in the area is generally easy, on wide roads across the plain, with the high Taurus mountains to the south and the river gorge to the east. Traffic around Malatya is dense, and trucks use the main roads heavily. The summer heat is very strong, and the best times are spring and autumn. Malatya, about five kilometres away, has fuel and every kind of service, so planning is not an issue. Buy a bag of apricots, fresh in June or dried at any time of year, and have a glass of tea with them.
t.nemrut dag@38.0,38.8:
On the summit of Nemrut Dağ, at a little over two thousand metres in the Taurus mountains of south-eastern Turkey, a king ordered his own sanctuary to be built, and the result is one of the strangest sights in the world. Antiochus I, ruler of the small kingdom of Commagene in the first century BC, wanted to be remembered among the gods. He had an artificial mound of crushed stone raised over his tomb, about fifty metres high, and in terraces on its east and west sides he set colossal seated statues, some eight to nine metres tall, of himself, of Greek and Persian gods, of a lion and an eagle. Over the centuries earthquakes and frost brought the heads tumbling off, and they now sit on the ground in rows, staring out across the terrace with calm stone faces.

The mix of gods reflects Commagene's position at the meeting of empires: Zeus is merged with the Persian Ahura Mazda, Apollo with Mithras, and Heracles with Ares, and the king claims descent from both Persian and Macedonian dynasties. The kingdom was swallowed by Rome in the following century, and the mountain was forgotten until a German engineer found it in 1881. The site is a World Heritage property, and people climb at sunrise and sunset, when the light turns the stone gold and the plains below fill with shadow.

Roads up the mountain wind through bare, rounded hills and small villages, and the last section to the car park is steep, with tight bends and a narrower surface, so it needs care. The road is generally open from about April or May to October, and snow can block it well into spring. Nights are cold even in summer, and the wind on the summit is sharp. Allow time for a short walk from the car park up the final slope, over loose stones.

Fuel is not available on the mountain. The larger towns are Kâhta, about thirty kilometres away, and Adıyaman, and Sincik has basic shops. Fill up before you start. On the way, the Roman Cendere Bridge, built for the emperor Septimius Severus, spans a gorge with three of its original four columns, and it is worth a stop.
t.vologda@59.2,39.9:
Vologda is a city of wooden lace curtains, church domes and slow rivers, and it has an air of unhurried self-respect that you do not find in bigger Russian places. About three hundred thousand people live here, on the Vologda river in the north of European Russia, and the city has been important since the sixteenth century, when Ivan the Terrible considered making it his capital. He built the Cathedral of St Sophia here, a great white building with five domes that still dominates the riverbank, and began a kremlin, though it was never completed to his plans.

The town's famous products are lace, butter and woodwork. Vologda lace, made on bobbins in patterns of flowers and geometric forms, has been known for centuries and is still made by hand, and you can buy it from craft shops. The butter was exported across Europe in the nineteenth century and the name is still used as a mark of quality. Wooden houses with carved window frames, called nalichniki, line the older streets, in shades of blue and green and bright white trim, and many have been restored.

Vologda was also a place of exile. Over the centuries the authorities sent a number of political prisoners here, including some who went on to become famous. Peter the Great visited and used the Vologda river as a route for shipping to the north, and a small house he used is preserved as a museum. The railway came in the nineteenth century, and the city remains an important junction.

As a ride, Vologda is a staging post. The roads out to the north lead to Kirillov and the monasteries beyond, a gentle country road through flat forest and farmland, with long straights and few curves. The surface can be broken by frost heaves, so watch for dips, and heavy trucks are frequent on the main route. The river and the ponds are surrounded by willows and birches.

Everything is in the city, from fuel and mechanics to hotels and restaurants. The local food is northern and rich, with fish pies, mushroom soup, dairy products and honey cake, and the tea is strong and well served. Summer evenings are long and warm, with church bells carrying across the river, and in winter the whole city sits under snow and the domes glitter in the cold.
t.torzhok@57.0,35.0:
Torzhok is an old trading town on the Tvertsa river, about sixty kilometres from Tver, and its name simply means the market. It was the grain gate of medieval Novgorod, a place where supplies from the Volga lands were assessed and taxed before moving north to the great city. That strategic role made it a target, and it was burned and sacked several times, once by the Mongol army in the thirteenth century. The town survived and grew, and in the eighteenth century it found a role on the road between Moscow and Saint Petersburg, hosting travellers who needed a change of horses.

That road gave Torzhok some of its fame. Pushkin stayed here more than once, and the town is known for a dish of minced chicken cutlets named after the family of innkeepers called Pozharsky, who, according to the legend, served them to Tsar Nicholas I on a journey. Whether or not the story is true, the cutlets are on every local menu and are delicious, tender and crispy at once. The town is also famous for its gold embroidery, made with metallic thread on velvet or silk in elaborate designs, a craft that goes back centuries and was used for church vestments and slippers. The museum shows beautiful examples.

Walking the old centre, you can see a number of historic churches and the walls of the Boris and Gleb Monastery, which has a cluster of white buildings and a tall bell tower overlooking the river. Torzhok has a gentle, lived-in air, with wooden houses, merchants' mansions and a riverside promenade where people stroll in the evening. The river is lined with willows, and in autumn the leaves float down the current.

For a rider, the landscape here is a gentle one of low rolling hills, fields and woodland, with the Valdai Hills rising to the west. The old main highway passes close by, and traffic can be heavy and fast, with trucks, though quieter local roads lead into the countryside. Surfaces are variable, and potholes and frost heaves appear in places. The light in September, with gold fields and clear air, is a pleasure.

Torzhok is large enough to have fuel, supermarkets and cafés, so it is a convenient place for a longer pause. The cutlets are the obvious choice for lunch, and some bakeries sell sweet pies. Mosquitoes in summer and snow in winter are the main inconveniences.
t.istra@55.9,36.9:
Istra is a Moscow Oblast town of about thirty-three thousand on the river of the same name, an hour or so west of the capital depending on how badly the Volokolamsk highway has behaved that day. Its great claim is the New Jerusalem Monastery, which stands on a bluff above the water and looks like a stage set for an entire other country. Patriarch Nikon founded it in the 1650s with the idea of recreating the holy places of Palestine in the Russian countryside, and the huge rotunda of its Resurrection Cathedral was modelled on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. The river was even renamed the Jordan, and nearby hills got names to match.

The monastery's later story is a reminder of how close the front came. In the Battle of Moscow in late 1941, German forces reached this area, and in December, as they fell back, they mined and blew up the cathedral. What you see today is the product of decades of restoration, and the soaring tented roofs and glazed tile decoration still look different in different light. Even if you do not go inside, ride past and look back at it from the road along the water.

The reservoir behind the town was created in the 1930s as part of the water system feeding the capital, and the roads around it wander through birch and pine woods, dacha villages and open fields. Surfaces are mixed. Main roads are wide and decent, and the lanes toward the shoreline can be patched, potholed and sandy in the shoulders, so keep your speed honest. Weekend traffic from Moscow is heavy, with long convoys heading to country houses, so a Sunday afternoon return is a very different thing to a Tuesday morning start. Look out for speed cameras, which are common on the main roads, and for dogs that wander the village streets.

Practically, Istra is large enough for fuel stations on the main roads and plenty of cafes serving soup, pelmeni and tea. Snegiri, about ten kilometres off, is smaller but sits on the same approaches, and for anything unusual you will probably need to head for Moscow itself. Give yourself an early start, take the side roads when you can, and leave time for the monastery walls at golden hour.
t.klin@56.3,36.7:
Klin is a working town of eighty thousand on the old road between Moscow and St Petersburg, and for a rider on a long day it is where the choice is turning back or pushing on toward Tver. The Leningrad highway runs right past, the railway too, and the town itself sits on rolling country at the edge of the Valdai hills, with the Sestra River slipping through.

The reason to remember it is Tchaikovsky. He settled in the Klin area in the 1880s, and the house where he lived and worked in his last years is now a museum, kept more or less as he left it, with his piano in the room. His final symphony was written here, and he died in 1893 not long after a visit to St Petersburg. Klin also has a long industrial history, and the glass Christmas ornaments made here are still part of the local identity. In a country that takes New Year seriously, that matters. If you want a souvenir that will survive a motorcycle pannier, a small glass bauble from a local shop is the safest bet you will find.

Riding around Klin, the pleasure is in the quieter roads. North of the main highway, the lanes toward Vysokovsk and the Dmitrov country cross low ridges, small rivers and big, empty fields. Corners are gentle rather than dramatic, the horizons are wide, and the villages are strung with wooden houses with painted window frames. Surfaces vary a lot. Good asphalt gives way to patched tar and sometimes gravel at the edges, so treat blind crests with respect. On the big highway, trucks are frequent and fast, and the wind sheet from a passing lorry can move you across your lane. Better to leave the trunk road at the first sensible exit.

Practically, a town this size has plenty of fuel and food, with cafes and shops near the centre and along the highway. Mornings are best, before traffic builds from the capital, and early autumn has a lovely clear light on the birch woods. In winter the whole area is under snow and the roads become a different problem. Allow time for the museum if you are a music person, because the quiet garden alone is worth a short break.
t.kenya lake system in the great rift vall:
The Kenya Lake System sits in the floor of the Great Rift Valley, the vast crack in the earth that runs from the Red Sea to Mozambique, and it is made up of three shallow soda lakes: Bogoria, Nakuru and Elementaita. UNESCO listed them in 2011 because of the birds. The alkaline water breeds a bloom of tiny blue-green algae, and the algae feed millions of lesser flamingos, which turn the shallows pink and, when they take off in a mass, fill the air with a roar of wings. Over a hundred species of other birds, including pelicans and eagles, share the shores.

The valley itself is the main spectacle. Coming from Nairobi, the road climbs through highland farms to the lip of the escarpment and then drops suddenly into a wide, hazy plain with extinct volcanoes standing in it, among them Longonot and Menengai. The floor of the rift is dry and open, with acacia thorn scrub and herds of zebra and gazelle, and the air is dry and sharp. Nakuru, twenty-four kilometres away, is Kenya's fourth-largest city, with fuel, restaurants and a National Park that is full of white rhinos and Rothschild's giraffes.
