The riding here is on the main A104, the old Nairobi to Uganda road, which is a busy and sometimes rough highway with heavy trucks, matatus overtaking on blind rises and unmarked speed bumps in the villages, so alertness matters. Sunrise is a lovely time, with mist in the hollows and the first light on the lake. Midday is hot, and in the afternoon thunderstorms can arrive quickly, particularly in the rainy seasons around April and November. Kenya drives on the left.

When you ride in the area, fill the tank in Nakuru or Gilgil, where you will find stations, and carry water. Roadside stalls sell roasted maize, mangoes and fresh milk, and you will find a decent meal in most towns. Carry cash, since card machines are unreliable, and take care at dusk, when livestock and pedestrians wander onto the road.
t.lake elementaita@-0.4,36.2:
Lake Elementaita is the smallest and quietest of the three soda lakes, a shallow stretch of pale water in the Rift Valley that looks, in the right light, like a sheet of beaten silver. The name comes from a Maasai word, muteita, which means a place of dust, and the dry, windy shore bears it out. Behind the lake rises a ridge called the Sleeping Warrior, whose outline resembles a man lying on his back, and local people tell the tale of the sleeping giant with a straight face.

The lake is a haven for birds. Flocks of lesser flamingos come and go with the algae, and great white pelicans nest on the rocky islets, in one of the main breeding places in the region. The land around it, the Soysambu Conservancy, was once part of the huge estate of Lord Delamere, an early British settler who became a leading figure of the colony, and it is now a wildlife area where zebra, giraffe and impala graze among the thorn trees. Hot springs seep along the shore, and in places the water steams.

On a motorbike, the ride to Elementaita is mostly a matter of the highway. From Nairobi you climb to the escarpment, with its great view over the rift, and then follow the A104 north-west through Naivasha and Gilgil, passing fields of flowers and vegetables and small trading towns. Trucks are heavy, and the road is narrow, so take care overtaking. Winds in the afternoon can be strong, and rain, when it comes, is heavy.

Nakuru, twenty-four kilometres away, has fuel, banks and plenty of food, and Gilgil, nearer, has small stations. Carry water and sunscreen, since shade is scarce. If you have time, the lakeshore lodges allow a walk at the water's edge, and a cold drink on a terrace with pelicans in view is a good way to end a day on the road. Dust and wind are part of the experience, so protect the camera.
t.yuryev polsky@56.5,39.7:
Yuryev-Polsky is a small town with a big church. It was founded in 1152 by Prince Yuri Dolgoruky, the same prince credited with founding Moscow, and the name means Yuri's town in the Field, a reference to the open plain known as the Opolye, a stretch of fertile farmland surrounded by forest. It lies in Vladimir Oblast, a short drive from Suzdal, and its quiet streets, old merchant houses and green squares give it a calm that large tourist towns lack.

The main attraction is the Cathedral of St. George, built in white stone in 1234. Its walls were once covered with carved reliefs of saints, animals, birds and plants, a tradition of white-stone carving that flourished in the Vladimir-Suzdal region. The cathedral partly collapsed in the fifteenth century, and the builder Vasily Yermolin put it back together in 1471 using the original stones, though some are in the wrong places and some sculptures are in a different order from their original arrangement. The result is a puzzle that fascinates historians and a building of rare beauty.

Close by, the Archangel Michael Monastery, with its fortress-like walls and towers, adds a sense of old defense. The town has several museums, including one in a former merchant house. The landscape around is open and rolling, with fields of wheat and sunflowers, patches of forest and small rivers. Roads here are quiet, with gentle bends and a mix of good and patchy surfaces, and traffic is light outside the summer weekends. The best months are May to September, when the fields are green and the days long. Spring thaws can leave potholes.

For riders, the road between Suzdal and Yuryev-Polsky is a pleasant backroad through villages, and the way on to Alexandrov offers more of the same. Services in the town are modest, with a fuel station, a few shops and small cafes, and it is wise to fill up in Suzdal or Vladimir. A few simple guesthouses offer rooms and home cooking, and local honey and pickles are sold in summer.

Stop in the cathedral courtyard and look at the stone carving in the afternoon light. The animals and saints seem to move as the shadows shift.
t.rybinsk@58.0,38.9:
Rybinsk is a Volga river port in Yaroslavl Oblast, where the city's history is written in grain, barges and water. It started as a fishing village, and its name comes from the Russian word for fish. By the nineteenth century it had become the main grain port of the upper Volga, where cargo from the south was transferred from large river boats to smaller vessels that could travel north through the canals to St. Petersburg. Thousands of men worked on the quays, and the city's warehouses and exchange building, a handsome brick structure that stands on the embankment, recall that boom.

The workers included the burlaks, the barge haulers who dragged vessels upstream along the riverbank with ropes, a job of famous misery. The painter Ilya Repin made them an icon of Russian suffering in his picture Barge Haulers on the Volga, and a monument to the burlaks stands on the Rybinsk waterfront. Another landmark is the great reservoir that spreads north of the city. The Rybinsk Reservoir, created in the early 1940s, was for a time the largest man-made lake in the world, and it drowned the old town of Mologa and many villages, which now lie under the water. In dry years, the old foundations sometimes emerge, a haunting sight.

The city is large, with over two hundred thousand people, a mix of industry and old buildings. It builds aircraft engines, and the Transfiguration Cathedral and the museum of local history are worth visiting. The embankment is pleasant for a walk in the evening. The surrounding country is gentle, with farmland and wood on either side of the Volga, and the roads are fairly flat and quiet, with long straight sections and occasional curves. The summer is warm, with a good chance of rain, and the autumn can be brilliant.

Fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes are everywhere, and Rybinsk is a reliable stop on the way to Uglich or Myshkin. A Volga fish, smoked or fried, is the natural thing to eat, and local places often serve it with potatoes and pickles.

Look at the river from the embankment in the late afternoon. The water is broad and slow, and the old warehouses glow in the light.
t.alexandrov@56.4,38.7:
Alexandrov is a town with a dark and fascinating past. In the sixteenth century it was the personal residence of Ivan the Terrible, who moved his court here in 1564 and made it the capital of the oprichnina, the terror regime in which he set up a private force to crush the boyars and, as he saw it, treason. From this place, the tsar ruled his country for seventeen years, and the Alexandrov Sloboda was the center of a system of fear. It is now a museum complex, the Alexandrov Kremlin, with a church, a bell tower, a refectory and the remains of fortifications, all tucked behind a wall in the middle of the town.

The chief monument is the Trinity Cathedral, built in the early sixteenth century and later redecorated, and the Assumption Convent, which was a center of religious life long before and after Ivan. One of the more poignant details is the connection to women. Several royal women were forced to take the veil here, and some are buried in the convent. In the twentieth century, the poet Marina Tsvetaeva spent time in the town, and the literary connection is remembered in a small museum.

The town lies on the border between Moscow and Vladimir regions, on gentle country of fields and forests, and it is a stop on the route of the Golden Ring of old Russian towns. The roads are mostly good, with moderate traffic, and the nearby back roads toward Suzdal, Yuryev-Polsky and Pereslavl are quiet and pleasant. Weekends in summer bring tour buses and Muscovites, so a weekday visit is calmer. Spring is muddy, and winter is cold and snowy.

Practical matters are easy. Alexandrov has about sixty thousand people, a number of fuel stations, shops and cafes, and a few hotels. It is a good place for a pause between Moscow and the Golden Ring towns to the north and east. The kremlin has opening hours and an entrance fee, and it is best to arrive in the morning.

Sit on a bench near the cathedral for a while. The silence behind the walls is thick, and the history seems to hang in the air.
t.rybinsk@58.0,38.8:
Rybinsk was built on one trade: moving grain up the Volga. In the nineteenth century this was the point where cargo from the big river boats was transferred onto smaller craft for the canal routes to St Petersburg, and every summer tens of thousands of barge haulers gathered on the embankment to sell the strength of their backs. The town grew rich on it, and the old grain exchange building on the waterfront, with its arcades and little towers, is the monument to that money. Next to it stands the Transfiguration Cathedral with a bell tower that rises high above the low skyline and is visible from far down the river.

The other great fact of Rybinsk is the dam. In the late 1930s and early 1940s the Soviet state built a hydroelectric plant just upstream and flooded a vast area behind it, creating the Rybinsk Reservoir, one of the largest artificial lakes in Europe. Whole villages and the old town of Mologa disappeared under the water, and the memory of that loss is kept in a small museum. Ride out to the dam and the sense of scale is startling: on a grey day the reservoir looks like an open sea.

As the finish of a ride down the Volga from Uglich and Myshkin, Rybinsk is a good place to end. The roads that bring you here run along or near the river through farmland and forest, mostly flat, with some rough surfaces and long straights where trucks set the pace. The town itself is busy with traffic, tram tracks and cobbles in places, so take the last few kilometres calmly. The embankment is wide and pleasant for an evening walk, with river boats tied up and old merchant houses facing the water.

Rybinsk has around two hundred thousand people, so fuel, workshops, hotels and restaurants are all easy to find. It is also an aircraft engine town, home to a big factory that has built engines for decades, which gives the place a practical, industrial feel under the old facades. If you have a free morning, the cathedral and the exchange are a short walk apart, and the view across the river from the embankment at sunset is the right way to close the day.
t.peski@55.2,38.8:
The name means sands, and it is honest: Peski sits on the sandy terraces of the Moskva River just before it joins the Oka, a landscape of pine woods, small dachas and quiet lanes where the soil drains fast and the trees smell of resin on a warm afternoon. It is a small settlement of a few thousand people in the southeast of Moscow Oblast, between the industrial town of Voskresensk upstream and the old fortress city of Kolomna downstream, along the railway line that runs from Moscow toward Ryazan.

For a rider this is a transition point. Behind you is the sprawl of the capital region, with its heavy traffic and endless roadworks; ahead, as you push toward Ryazan and the poet Sergei Yesenin's home village of Konstantinovo on the Oka, the country opens out into river meadows, fields and long views. The roads around Peski are local ones, narrow and often patched, threading through pine forest and past summer cottages, with the occasional sandy shoulder that can catch a careless wheel. Weekday mornings are quiet; Friday afternoons in summer bring the dacha exodus out of Moscow.

Kolomna, a short ride east, is the place to stop properly. It has one of the best preserved kremlins in the Moscow region, with massive red brick walls and towers from the sixteenth century, and it is famous for pastila, a light, airy confection made from baked apples and egg white whipped together and dried. There are small museums devoted to it, and boxes of the stuff make a good present that weighs almost nothing in a tank bag.

In Peski itself, expect basic shops and not much more. For fuel and a wider choice of food, Voskresensk is about thirteen kilometres away and has everything you need, and Kolomna is not much further. The river banks nearby are popular for swimming in summer, sandy and shallow in places, with locals grilling shashlik on weekends. It is not a grand stop, but in the evening light, with long shadows through the pines and the river slipping past, it has a gentle, unhurried appeal.
t.yegoryevsk@55.4,39.0:
Ride into Yegoryevsk from almost any direction and the first thing you see is the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, a huge, ornate church whose domes and towers dominate the low skyline like something dropped in from a much bigger city. It was built in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century with money from local textile merchants, and it is the kind of building that tells you exactly where the money in this town came from: cotton mills, weaving and trade, run by merchant dynasties who competed in piety as much as in business.

Yegoryevsk, named for Saint George, sits on the western edge of Meshchera in the southeast of Moscow Oblast. It has around eighty-five thousand people and still feels like a provincial industrial town, with old red brick factory buildings, wide streets and a mix of merchant houses and Soviet apartment blocks. There is a local history museum in a merchant's mansion, and the old trading rows near the centre are worth a slow look. Around the town the land is flat, with pine and birch forest, peat bogs and old phosphorite workings that left lakes and scarred ground.

The riding here is the gateway kind. From Yegoryevsk the roads head east into the forest country of Meshchera, long and mostly straight, with occasional bends around lakes or villages and a surface that varies from fresh asphalt to rippled, patched tarmac. Logging trucks and slow farm traffic are common. In summer the forest smells wonderful but the mosquitoes and horseflies near the bogs are fierce. In dry years the peat bogs have been known to smoulder, and the haze can drift across the roads.

As a stop, Yegoryevsk is straightforward and useful. Fuel stations, supermarkets, cafes and canteens are easy to find, and there are a few hotels. If you are heading deeper into Meshchera, this is a good place to fill up and buy water, because the villages ahead are small and the distances between services grow. Stand in front of the cathedral for a minute; it is one of the more surprising buildings in the region.
t.zhukovo@55.0,36.7:
This town on the Protva River carries the name of Georgy Zhukov, the Soviet marshal who commanded at Moscow, Stalingrad and Berlin and is probably the most famous Russian soldier of the twentieth century. He was born in a peasant house in the village of Strelkovka, a few kilometres away, and the area has made much of him: there is a museum dedicated to his life, a monument, and the town itself was renamed in his honour in the 1990s. It has around twelve thousand people and the quiet, practical air of a district centre.

The Protva valley is pleasant country, with the river winding between wooded banks, meadows and small villages. Just to the north lies Obninsk, the science city where the world's first nuclear power station for civilian grid use was switched on in the 1950s; it is now a museum, and the town is full of research institutes. Between these two places the landscape is surprisingly green, with pine forest and birch groves, and the river attracts fishermen and summer swimmers.

For riders, Zhukovo works as an early stop on a route heading south toward Kaluga and the Ugra River. The roads around here are typical of the Kaluga region, a mixture of decent main roads with trucks and narrower country lanes with patched surfaces, gentle curves and a few hills where the road dips to cross a stream. In autumn the colours along the Protva are lovely, and on a clear day in early summer the light is long and soft well into the evening.

The practical side is simple. Fuel stations, shops and cafes are easy to find in town, and Obninsk, about eleven kilometres north, has the full range of services, from supermarkets to workshops. If you want to see the Zhukov museum, it is small and well kept, with personal belongings and wartime material, and gives a sense of how far one peasant boy from these fields travelled. Afterwards, the riverbank is a good place for a quiet break before heading on toward Kaluga.
t.tallahassee@30.4,-84.3:
Tallahassee became the capital of Florida in 1824 for a reason that had nothing to do with beauty: it lay roughly halfway between the two old colonial towns of Pensacola and St. Augustine, which made it a fair meeting point for legislators travelling by horseback. The result is a capital that feels a world away from beach Florida. It sits among red clay hills and pine woods in the Panhandle, closer in spirit to Georgia than to Miami, and its population of nearly two hundred thousand is dominated by government workers and students from Florida State and Florida A&M universities.

The city's great gift to riders is its canopy roads. Several old routes leading out of town have been protected so that the live oaks on either side meet overhead, festooned with Spanish moss, forming long green tunnels. Roads such as Centerville, Miccosukee, Old St. Augustine and Meridian are narrow, gently curving and lovely, especially in the morning when the light filters through. Treat them gently, since there is little room for error and some sections are popular with cyclists.

In the centre, the old Capitol, a restored nineteenth-century building with striped awnings and a dome, stands in front of the modern twenty-two-storey tower that replaced it, a contrast that locals have plenty of opinions about. South of the city, Wakulla Springs is one of the largest and deepest freshwater springs in the world, where Tarzan films and Creature from the Black Lagoon were shot, and where you can still see manatees, alligators and herons from a river boat. Further on, the St. Marks lighthouse stands on the edge of the Gulf in a wildlife refuge famous for migrating monarch butterflies in autumn.

As the start of the Big Bend Scenic Byway, Tallahassee is the place to sort out everything: fuel, food, repairs, supplies. Once you head toward the coast, the towns become small and far apart. The climate is hot and humid from May to September, with almost daily afternoon thunderstorms, and winter can surprise visitors with frosty mornings. Spring, with azaleas blooming in March and April, is the nicest time to be here.
t.near arusha@-3.4,36.7:
Mount Meru gives Arusha a backdrop that most cities would envy. The volcano rises to about 4,500 metres directly behind the town, a jagged crater rim you see on clear mornings and lose in cloud by afternoon, while Kilimanjaro floats above the horizon to the east. Arusha itself sits at around 1,400 metres on fertile volcanic soil, with coffee farms, banana groves and flower plantations on the surrounding slopes. It is a busy, dusty, friendly town of more than 300,000 people, the gateway for safaris to the northern parks, and the place where the Arusha Declaration of 1967 laid out Tanzania's socialist policies under Julius Nyerere. The Maasai are a constant presence, in their red shuka cloths, selling beads and herding cattle on the edge of town.

Leaving Arusha westward, the road, the A104, runs across a plain, past the Maasai steppe, and then climbs the wall of the Rift Valley near Lake Manyara. The road is generally good tarmac, but trucks and buses are heavy, and Tanzanian drivers take risks on blind curves, so patience matters. From the escarpment, the view over the lake and the rift floor is huge, and the colour of the light changes by the hour.

A very important note concerns the national parks. Tanzania charges substantial fees to enter Ngorongoro and Serengeti, and the rules for motorbikes in those areas are strict, as riding in wildlife areas is generally not allowed for visitors. Anyone planning this route should check with park authorities and tour operators well ahead, because a trip may need to be done in a vehicle with a guide. Dangerous animals, including lions, buffalo and elephants, are real, and not something to meet on a motorcycle.

Fuel, supplies and repair shops are plentiful in Arusha, so fill the tank, check the bike and buy water before leaving. Try nyama choma, grilled meat with kachumbari salad, at a local bar, and Kilimanjaro or Safari beer. The dry seasons, June to October and January to February, are best, while April and May bring heavy rain that turns dirt roads to mud.
